Abstract:
Laser powder-bed fusion (LPBF) has significantly gained in importance and has become one of the major fabrication techniques within metal additive manufacturing. The fast cooling rates achieved in LPBF due to a relatively small melt pool on a much larger component or substrate, acting as heat sink, result in fine-grained microstructures and high oversaturation of alloying elements in the α-aluminum. Al–Si–Mg alloys thus can be effectively precipitation hardened. Moreover, the solidified material undergoes an intrinsic heat treatment, whilst the layers above are irradiated and the elevated temperature in the built chamber starts the clustering process of alloying elements directly after a scan track is fabricated. These silicon–magnesium clusters were observed with atom probe tomography in as-built samples. Similar beneficial clustering behavior at higher temperatures is known from the direct-aging approach in cast samples, whereby the artificial aging is performed immediately after solution annealing and quenching. Transferring this approach to LPBF samples as a possible post-heat treatment revealed that even after direct aging, the outstanding hardness of the as-built condition could, at best, be met, but for most instances it was significantly lower. Our investigations showed that LPBF Al–Si–Mg exhibited a high dependency on the quenching rate, which is significantly more pronounced than in cast reference samples, requiring two to three times higher quenching rate after solution annealing to yield similar hardness results. This suggests that due to the finer microstructure and the shorter diffusion path in Al–Si–Mg fabricated by LPBF, it is more challenging to achieve a metastable oversaturation necessary for precipitation hardening. This may be especially problematic in larger components.

Abstract:
<jats:p>The influence of base plate temperature (25, 100, 200, and 400 °C) on the laser powder bed fusion processing of EN AW 7075 was systematically investigated using microstructural characterisation (LM, SEM, EBSD, GROD), chemical analysis, hardness testing, and thermal simulations across a broad range of process parameters. Moderate preheating at 100 °C and 200 °C showed no significant reduction in crack density or changes in grain morphology compared to processing without preheating. At the highest studied temperature—400 °C—a transition to columnar crack networks was observed, accompanied by modified grain orientation, pronounced stress relaxation, and reduced hardness. Independent of preheating temperature, consistent evaporation of Zn (~1 wt.%) and Mg (~0.3 wt.%) occurred during processing. Thermal simulations qualitatively supported the experimental observations, indicating increased thermal retention and displacement with increasing preheating temperature. The results demonstrate that base plate preheating alone is insufficient to suppress hot cracking in EN AW 7075 and may promote alternative crack-growth mechanisms at elevated temperatures, highlighting the need for alternative alloy or process design strategies.</jats:p>

Abstract:
The report presents the microstructure and mechanical properties of 3D printed Inconel 718 after irradiation in the High Flux Isotope Reactor (HFIR) at Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) to assess its potential use as a structural material. The structural components near the outlets of several proposed reactor cores will experience significant neutron fluxes and outlet coolant temperatures ranging from the hot standby temperature of 300 °C to nearly 550 °C at the center of the part. These components must support the core in appropriate loading conditions and require structural analysis at relevant temperatures. In FY21, three heat treatments were designed and conducted to simplify the microstructure and to determine how each precipitating phase contributed to the overall strength. In FY21, baseline mechanical properties were measured from uniaxial tensile tests on subsize SS-J2 specimens at room temperature and at elevated temperatures of 300, 450, and 600 °C to serve a comparison to the irradiated properties. Four capsules containing 3D printed Inconel 718 were inserted into HFIR in FY21 for a matrix of two temperatures and two doses. The lower of the two doses was available for characterization in FY22. Multiple heat treatments of Inconel 718 irradiated to nominal conditions of 2 displacements per atom (dpa) at either 300 or 600 °C were strained with uniaxial tensile tests at the Irradiated Material Examination and Testing (IMET) Facility to discern the mechanical properties. Transmission electron microscopy was performed to correlate the observed mechanical properties with nanoscale features. The initially homogenous AM718-HM increased in strength at both irradiation temperatures based on a high density of nanometer-scale radiation-induced cavities at lower temperature and nucleation and growth of γ ʺ precipitates at higher temperatures. The precipitate-hardened AM718-HT2 showed very small differences in strength before and after irradiation: the contribution to strength from γ ʺ precipitates was replaced with dislocation loops. Because the radioactivity of the nickel superalloys from neutron activation limited the scope of the analysis, a feasibility study examined the possibility of an ultra-miniature specimen geometry, colloquially SS-Tiny (SS-T), for mechanical property determination using the nonirradiated Inconel 718. This study found an overestimation of ductility from the SS-T geometry with yield strength and ultimate tensile strength slightly above the SS-J2 geometry: this could be contributed to a reduction in specimen thickness.

                  <jats:p>Laser Powder Bed Fusion (L-PBF) has emerged as a transformative additive manufacturing technique, offering the capability to fabricate complex geometries and customized components directly from digital models. Its application in producing H13 tool steel dies for hot work tooling presents a promising alternative to conventional manufacturing. This study investigates the influence of laser scanning speed (ranging from 150 to 600 mm/s) and subsequent multi-stage heat treatments including annealing, quenching, tempering, and double tempering on the microstructure and mechanical performance of L-PBF-processed H13 steel. The results indicate that increasing scan speed leads to higher martensite content but adversely affects tensile strength and hardness. In contrast, the annealing stage refined the microstructure, enhancing ductility and promoting phase homogenization. While quenching followed by tempering improved toughness and wear resistance, it was accompanied by a reduction in tensile strength. Notably, a 1200% increase in impact toughness was observed after tempering at the lowest scan speed, despite a slight decrease in wear resistance. The microstructural evolution, porosity levels, and phase transformations are comprehensively analyzed to explain the observed trends, guiding the optimization of L-PBF and heat treatment parameters for tooling applications.</jats:p>

Abstract:

 Laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) Ti-6Al-4 V parts exhibit variable fatigue strength due to inherent processing defects such as high residual stress, rough surface finish, subsurface and internal pores, and a brittle metastable microstructure. Traditional models often fail to predict this fatigue strength accurately due to the complexities involved. This study employs machine learning (ML) to analyze the sensitivity of various input features on fatigue strength predictions for LPBF-produced Ti-6Al-4 V parts. Through feature sensitivity analysis and testing of different feature selection methods, critical predictors such as surface roughness, stress intensity factor (ΔK
 th), hot isostatic pressure (HIP) and elongation at break were identified. Utilizing a comprehensive dataset derived from 55 studies, a gradient boosting decision tree model was refined through feature selection, demonstrating a prediction accuracy with an R
 2 of 80%. Moreover, incorporating these sensitive features into ML models significantly enhances prediction reliability and offers insights into the critical factors affecting fatigue strength in LPBF. This research also contributes to the understanding of feature selection in the context of additive manufacturing.

Abstract:
<jats:p>This paper presents an experimental study on the influence of the main Laser Powder Bed Fusion (PBF-LB) process parameters on the density and surface quality of the IN 625 superalloy manufactured using the Lasertec 30 SLM machine. Parameters’ influence was investigated within a workspace defined by the laser power (150–400 W), scanning speed (500–900 m/s), scanning strategy (90° and 67°), layer thickness (30–70 µm), and hatch distance (0.09–0.12 µm). Experimental results showed that laser power and scanning speed play a determining role in producing a relative density higher than 99.5% of the material’s theoretical density. A basic set of process parameters was selected for generating high-density material: laser power 250 W, laser speed 750 mm/s, layer thickness 40 µm, and hatch distance 0.11 mm. The 67° scanning strategy ensures higher roughness surfaces than the 90° scanning strategy, roughness that increases as the laser power increases and the laser speed decreases.</jats:p>

From text 'wilsnack2023fabricationofan pages 1-3'.

C Wilsnack, J Moritz, A Reutlinger, and S Eberle. Fabrication of an athermal mirror from a hyper-eutectic alsi alloy via lpbf. Unknown journal, 2023.

The excerpt provides only partial LPBF parameters for AlSi40 on an Aconity Mini machine; it does not identify an Aconity MIDI or LAB machine. The Aconity Mini used a 1064 nm ytterbium fiber laser with a maximum laser power of 200 W, argon shielding gas, a build chamber of Ø98 × 130 mm³, and substrate preheating capability up to 800 °C. The process study initially tested 500 °C substrate preheating, but this produced defect accumulations and pores in the lower specimen layers. Subsequent experiments used 400 °C preheating, together with redesigned supports to improve heat transport, and produced a more homogeneous pore distribution. The excerpt does not report numerical scan speed, hatch distance, layer thickness, or scan strategy values. It also does not provide a quantitative density value or percentage; it only states that the 500 °C trials had acceptable overall density and that lowering the preheat improved pore uniformity. The AlSi40 powder particle-size fraction was 20–63 µm. These are the only machine and process details available in the supplied pages.

However, the excerpt does not report the resulting density value numerically. It identifies layer thickness and scan strategy as important LPBF parameters, but gives no specific layer-thickness value for this experiment. Scan strategies discussed include unidirectional, bidirectional, and checkerboard patterns, with scan orientation potentially rotated 90° between layers; these are general descriptions rather than confirmed settings for the cited density result. No preheat temperature is provided. The excerpt also does not identify whether the parameters were used on an Aconity MIDI, MINI, or LAB machine. It notes that process parameters and scanning strategy affect microstructure, porosity, surface quality, and mechanical properties. In particular, the lowest energy-density specimen had the highest porosity and lowest part density, while narrow hatch spacing could cause overlapping scan tracks and additional reheating cycles. Thus, only laser power, scan speed, and hatch distance can be extracted quantitatively from this passage, and machine-specific details, preheating, layer thickness, scan strategy assignment, and numerical density require another source or the omitted continuation.

The excerpt describes general LPBF parameters but does not provide specific settings for Aconity MIDI, MINI, or LAB machines, nor does it report resulting density values for aluminum alloys. It states that LPBF laser parameters include laser power, spot size, and scan speed; typical scan speeds are 100–1000 mm/s. Hatch distance is identified as the spacing between adjacent laser scans, and overlap between scan tracks is recommended to improve bonding, but no numerical hatch-distance values are given. The available LPBF layer thickness is reported as 20–100 µm, although this is a general machine capability rather than an Aconity-specific setting. LPBF normally does not require preheating, but the build platform may be heated to reduce residual stresses, delamination, and poor powder adhesion; no preheat temperature is specified. Scan strategy is described qualitatively: long scanning lines can increase residual stress, while rotating patterns can improve track overlap and powder consolidation. The excerpt also notes that LPBF optimization involves approximately 50 process parameters and that a suitable combination is needed for fully dense components. ## 1. Process and Properties of Al-Mg-Er-Zr-Sc High-Strength Aluminum Alloy Powder Prepared by Vacuum Induction Melting Gas Atomization

Abstract:
The Er-Zr-Sc-modified Al-Mg alloys produced by additive manufacturing (AM) exhibit good formability and excellent mechanical properties, and present great potential for applications in the fields of aerospace and automotive fields. In this work, the preparation process of Al-4.5Mg-0.7Er-0.5Zr-0.3Sc high-strength aluminum alloy powder for additive manufacturing by vacuum induction melting gas atomization (VIGA) was investigated. With the goal of obtaining excellent sphericity and higher powder yield in the particle size range of 15~53 μm, a new type atomizer with optimized convergence angle and tube extension length was designed based on finite element numerical simulation and experimental research, and the optimal atomization processing parameters were determined. The results revealed that when the convergence angle was 32° and the extension length was 5 mm, the large negative pressure and suction force at the tube outlet could facilitate the smooth flow of the melt and a refined powder particle size; when the melt temperature was 800 °C and the atomization pressure was 3.25 Mpa, the melt had low viscosity and the atomization gas could fully interact with the melt. Meanwhile, the melt droplets had suitable cooling conditions, avoiding the generation of irregular powders and improving the powder sphericity. Under the above optimal processing parameters, the prepared powders were spherical or nearly spherical with fine particle size and a high yield of about 39.45%.

## 2. Microstructural Evaluation and Tensile Properties of Al-Mg-Sc-Zr Alloys Prepared by LPBF
Valid Text Names:
'lu2023microstructuralevaluationand pages 1-2', 'lu2023microstructuralevaluationand pages 2-4', 'lu2023microstructuralevaluationand pages 4-6', 'lu2023microstructuralevaluationand pages 6-9', 'lu2023microstructuralevaluationand pages 9-10', 'lu2023microstructuralevaluationand pages 10-12', 'lu2023microstructuralevaluationand pages 12-13', 'lu2023microstructuralevaluationand pages 13-14'

    year = "2023",

    issue = "6",
    issn = "2073-4352"
}


Abstract:
Laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) is a typical additive manufacturing technology that offers significant advantages in the production of complex components. With the rapid heating and cooling characteristics of LPBF, a large amount of solid solution of alloying elements in the matrix can be achieved to form supersaturated solid solutions, thus enhancing the properties of LPBF alloys. For the unique microstructure, the heat treatment process needs to be adjusted accordingly. In this work, a Zr/Sc-modified Al-Mg alloy processed by laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) with relatively low cost and good mechanical properties was investigated. The fine microstructure was obtained under rapid solidification conditions. The nanoscale Al3(Sc,Zr) particles precipitated at the molten pool boundary during solidification. These particles, as effective heterogeneous nucleators, further refined the α-Al grains and improved the mechanical properties of the alloy. As a result, the alloy exhibited a heterogeneous microstructure consisting of columnar grains in the center of the molten pool and equiaxed grains at the boundaries. The rapid solidification resulted in the supersaturation of solute atoms in the α-Al matrix, which significantly enhanced the solid solution strengthening effect. With the LPBF processing parameters of a combination of a laser power of 250 W, a laser scanning speed of 833 mm/s, and stripe scanning mode, the tensile strength of the alloy reached 401.4 ± 5.7 MPa, which was significantly higher than that of the cast alloys with aging treatment (281.1 ± 1.3 MPa). The heat treatment promoted the formation of secondary Al3(Sc,Zr), Mn/Mg-rich phases. The ultimate tensile strength and elongation at fracture after aging at 325 °C for 2 h were 536.0 ± 1.7 MPa and 14.8 ± 0.8%, respectively. The results provide insight into the preparation of aluminum alloys with relatively low cost and excellent mechanical properties.

From text 'schimback2024advancementsinmetal pages 1-2'.

D. Schimbäck, L. Kaserer, P. Mair, M.S. Mohebbi, P. Staron, V. Maier-Kiener, I. Letofsky-Papst, T. Kremmer, F. Palm, I. Montes, H.W. Höppel, G. Leichtfried, and S. Pogatscher. Advancements in metal additive manufacturing: in-situ heat treatment of aluminium alloys during the laser powder bed fusion process. Jul 2024. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.msea.2024.146102, doi:10.1016/j.msea.2024.146102. This article has 32 citations.

The supplied excerpt identifies the LPBF system as an Aconity Midi equipped with a 1000 W Yb:YAG laser, but it does not state the actual laser power selected for the builds. It also does not provide the requested scan speed, hatch distance, layer thickness, or resulting part density; those values must be obtained from the remainder of the article, most likely the detailed LPBF-process methodology or parameter table. The excerpt does establish the platform-heating comparison: specimens were produced without build-platform heating (NoBPH) and with the platform heated to 200 °C (BPH). The 200 °C condition was deliberately used to promote dense Al-Sc-Zr solute-cluster formation during processing. According to the text, these clusters produced high strength directly in the as-built Scalmalloy state, eliminating the need for a subsequent heat-treatment cycle. The article also notes that conventional peak aging generally requires temperatures above 300 °C, while cluster formation in Sc(-Zr)-modified aluminium alloys has been observed around 250 °C. Thus, platform preheating is presented as a means of in-situ thermal treatment and improved as-built strength, rather than merely a strategy for densification. No quantitative density result or direct numerical comparison between the NoBPH and 200 °C BPH conditions is included in the provided pages.

## pqac-00000008

From text 'mehta2022al–mn–cr–zrbasedalloystailored pages 10-10'.

Bharat Mehta, Lars Nyborg, Karin Frisk, and Eduard Hryha. Al–mn–cr–zr-based alloys tailored for powder bed fusion-laser beam process: alloy design, printability, resulting microstructure and alloy properties. Journal of Materials Research, 37:1256-1268, Mar 2022. URL: https://doi.org/10.1557/s43578-022-00533-1, doi:10.1557/s43578-022-00533-1. This article has 22 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt reports LPBF-LB processing windows for nitrogen-atomized Al–Mn–Cr–Zr alloy powders with a nominal particle size of 20–53 µm. The baseline process used a 170 W laser power, 0.03 mm layer thickness, and 67° scan rotation. Hatch distance and laser speed were varied in a DOE to identify high-density conditions. For Alloys A and B, laser power was fixed at 170 W, hatch distance ranged from 0.10–0.15 mm, and laser speed ranged from 500–1500 mm/s. Alloy C used a broader laser-power range of 100–170 W, hatch distance of 0.10–0.15 mm, and laser speed of 500–2000 mm/s. The DOE targeted approximately 99.5% relative density; the excerpt does not provide a single measured density for each parameter combination. Powder was dried at 353 K for 4 h before printing. Regarding aging, as-printed material retained most alloying elements in solid solution, preserving an intended age-hardening response. Mn-rich nanometric precipitates formed at meltpool boundaries and were considered beneficial. Precipitate growth was slow during direct aging, strengthening the Al matrix. Higher Mn and Cr increased solid-solution strengthening while maintaining precipitation resistance up to 523 K; precipitation strengthening could be activated at higher temperatures, with 678 K given as an example, and occurred relatively slowly, suggesting potential for improved peak hardness and high-temperature properties.

The excerpt establishes that increasing the LPBF build-platform temperature from 35°C to 200°C changes the thermal gradient and therefore the AlSi10Mg microstructure. The Si-rich eutectic phase forms an interconnected network in the fine and coarse melt-pool zones, and this network contributes to strengthening by carrying load and hindering dislocation motion. Thermal input is expected to coarsen and globularise this network, reducing its strengthening effect and thereby weakening the material. In the reported comparison, the mean melt-pool size was broadly similar at 35°C and 200°C, but the heat-affected zone and coarse melt-pool zone were each approximately twice as thick at 200°C, producing a melt-pool border of double thickness. The excerpt does not provide the quantitative results needed to determine the full effects of 200°C preheating on Si-network coarsening, tensile strength, ductility, residual stress, or density. It also does not state direct residual-stress or density comparisons. Thus, it supports an expected coarsening/weakening trend and a clear change in melt-pool substructure, but not definitive numerical conclusions for all properties asked about.

The excerpt does not report experiments using a 200 °C build plate, nor does it provide a direct comparison of 200 °C preheating with no preheating for Si-network coarsening, residual stress, or density. Its relevant comparison is between an ambient platform and a 150 °C platform. At 150 °C, preheating causes in-situ precipitation of granular or rod-shaped Si and needle-like β'' precipitates. The authors attribute the increased strength primarily to the needle-like β'' phase, not to the Si phase. Preheating also changes the response to subsequent T5 ageing: ambient-platform material shows significant age hardening, whereas the 150 °C material shows only marginal additional age hardening; after T5, their mechanical properties become similar. The excerpt states that T5 ageing increases yield and tensile strength but reduces ductility, while an RST-T6 treatment substantially improves ductility and lowers tensile strength while maintaining yield strength for the 150 °C material. Therefore, the supplied text cannot establish the specific effects of 200 °C preheating on Si-network coarsening, strength, ductility, residual stress, or density relative to no preheating.

                         ABSTRACT

New aluminium alloy design strategies for laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) are needed to target
high strength and conductivity applications and substitute the traditional 6xxx series which
suffers from hot cracking during LPBF processing. This study presents the route followed to
design a novel Al-Fe-Zr alloy offering good processability, superior yield strength (310 MPa)
and thermal conductivity (180 W/m·K) after direct ageing (400°C/4h). The multi-scale
characterization, combining scanning and transmission electron microscopy with automated
crystallographic  orientation mapping and  energy  dispersive  spectroscopy,  reveals  the
precipitation of plate-like Al13Fe4 and coherent Al3Zr-L12 nanoprecipitates upon ageing,
enhancing the material’s strength. In turn, the associated solid solution depletion results in a
significant conductivity increase. The strategy to select low vapour pressure elements and slow
diffusers in Al, as well as the low solubility of Fe in Al demonstrates the ability through alloy
design for additive manufacturing to fill gaps in the material property space.

Keywords: Additive manufacturing; Laser powder bed fusion; Alloy design; Aluminium
alloys; mechanical performance; electrical conductivity.

      Combining low  density,  high  corrosion  resistance and  desirable  physical and
mechanical properties, Al-alloys are a workhorse of the transport and energy industries. Laser
powder bed fusion (LPBF) offers new perspectives to achieve near-net shape complex
components in few manufacturing steps, compared to the traditional routes of cast and wrought
products.
The preferred approach to produce Al-based LPBF components has been to use casting alloys
[1], for example AlSi7Mg and AlSi10Mg. Unfortunately, these grades do not deliver high
mechanical performance when LPBF-processed [2,3]. Al-alloys from the 6xxx series provide
both good strength and conductivity after a T6 heat-treatment and would be excellent
candidates to manufacture heat exchangers. However, they suffer from hot cracking during
autogenous laser welding because of their large freezing range and coefficient of thermal
expansion [4], and hot cracking also occurs during LPBF [5–8]. Uddin et al.[9] managed to
suppress hot cracking using powder bed heating to 500°C. Despite its success, this approach is
not compatible with industrial LPBF systems. Besides, adjustments to the alloy composition
have been considered, with addition of grain refiners that promote the heterogeneous nucleation
of Al grains, making the alloy more resistant to cracking. These refiners can either be
inoculating agents admixed to the powder like TiB2 and TiC [10,11], or primary phases formed
in situ such as Al3X (X=Zr, Sc) [5,6,8,12]. In this case, the benefit is two-fold with the
additional potential for precipitation strengthening through post-ageing treatment [13,14]. It
has also been suggested to tune the powder composition to favour elements which do not
increase the solidification range [15,16]. These approaches have addressed to some extent the
cracking issues of the 6xxx series. But other challenges remain, connected to laser-induced
solute evaporation and the need for further solutionizing and quenching. Briefly, there is a
necessity to develop novel Al-alloys with strength and conductivity comparable or surpassing
that of the 6xxx series combined with good LPBF processability.
This work introduces a new Al-alloy designed for LPBF to achieve a superior strength –
conductivity trade-off, by leveraging the unique characteristics of the process: the relatively
high solid-liquid interface velocities and high thermal gradients resulting in high cooling rates.
The multiscale characterization reveals unique microstructural features of the Al-Fe-Zr alloy
inherited from LPBF and their evolution upon ageing, further connected to the material tensile
response and conductivity.
     One criterion for alloying element selection is a low vapour pressure in comparison to
common solutes like Zn and Mg, which tend to restrict the processing window to low energy
inputs. The loss of such elements can lead to local composition variations and for example
reduced precipitation hardening for 6xxx or 7xxx alloys. Their vaporization can affect the melt
pool stability, lead to porosity formation, and generated vapours may interact with the laser,
resulting in diminished and varying energy input. These challenges will become more
predominant as production capacities are boosted with high power, multi-laser systems, and
high layer thicknesses [17]. An additional criterion is to favour elements with low diffusivity
in Al to limit the extent of in situ precipitation during thermal cycles and retain a supersaturated
solution in the as-built state. Finally, toxic elements such as Be are avoided as well as certain
Critical Raw Materials (CRMs) like Sc bringing high costs and supply risks.
      With these criteria, Zr and Fe were shortlisted as they combine both low vapour
pressure and low diffusivity in solid Al. Zr plays a dual role with the formation of primary
Al3Zr resulting in grain refinement, limiting hot cracking, and its contribution to precipitation
strengthening through post-ageing treatment [18]. It diffuses in Al more slowly than Sc [19].

## pqac-00000034

From text 'belelli2022investigationandcharacterization pages 8-14'.

F. Belelli, R. Casati, C. Andrianopoli, F. Cuccaro, and M. Vedani. Investigation and characterization of an al-mg-zr-sc alloy with reduced sc content for laser powder bed fusion. Journal of Alloys and Compounds, 924:166519, Nov 2022. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jallcom.2022.166519, doi:10.1016/j.jallcom.2022.166519. This article has 42 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt provides direct-aging information for an LPBF Al-Mg-Zr-Sc alloy with reduced Sc content, which may be relevant as a Sc-containing comparison but is not a complete dataset for all alloys listed in the question. Aging treatments were investigated at 300, 350, 375, and 400 °C. The strongest explicitly reported response was aging at 350 °C for 24 h, which increased hardness from 105 HV in the as-built condition to 160 HV. At 375 and 400 °C, comparable peak hardness of approximately 155 HV was reached after 8 h. The excerpt does not report the corresponding yield strengths, nor does it provide direct-aging schedules or resulting properties for AlSi10Mg, conventional Scalmalloy, Al-Mn-Cr-Zr, Al-Fe-Zr, or Al-Ce alloys. Mechanistically, the hardness increase is associated with precipitation of continuous and discontinuous L12-Al3(Sc,Zr) particles. Simulations predicted Al3(Sc,Zr) precipitation during aging and no secondary Al3Zr precipitates under the modeled conditions. The study also describes a four-stage precipitation sequence—nucleation, growth, transition, and coarsening—and indicates that lower supersaturation promotes earlier coarsening. Therefore, the supplied excerpt supports only the Al-Mg-Zr-Sc hardness schedule; additional alloy-specific literature is needed to establish comparable temperature/time treatments and yield strengths for the other alloy systems.

The excerpt provides direct-aging data only for LPBF Scalmalloy®, not for AlSi10Mg, Al-Mn-Cr-Zr, Al-Fe-Zr, or Al-Ce alloys. For Scalmalloy®, 325 °C is the most commonly used direct-aging temperature, with 4 h identified as the standard schedule. Reported hardness outcomes include 145 ± 4 HB after 325 °C/1 h and 125 ± 10 HV after 325 °C/5 h. Mechanical-property improvements were reported for 325 °C treatments lasting 4–16 h: ultimate tensile strength increased from 325 to 400 MPa, while yield strength increased from 260 to 350 MPa. Aging at 275 °C for 0.5–20 h was insufficient to reach peak aging. At 375 °C, peak-aging hardness was reached rapidly, after approximately 0.5 h, but over-aging became observable after 10 h. The excerpt also notes that 300 °C/2 h and 350 °C/4 h can increase grain size, while 400 °C/1 h produces fine, homogeneous Al3Sc precipitation; it does not provide corresponding hardness or yield-strength values for those schedules.

From text 'juhasz2020inandexsitu pages 104-109'.

MJ Juhasz. In and ex-situ process development in laser-based additive manufacturing. Unknown journal, 2020.

The excerpt provides only partial heat-treatment information, primarily for LPBF AlSi10Mg, and does not give direct-aging schedules or resulting hardness/yield-strength values for Scalmalloy, Al-Mn-Cr-Zr, Al-Fe-Zr, or Al-Ce alloys. For AlSi10Mg, the commonly cited stress-relief treatment is 300°C for 2 hours; lower treatments of 240–250°C reportedly increase ductility while producing little or no visible microstructural change, although the extent of residual-stress reduction remains unverified. The conventional precipitation-hardening route consists of stress relief, furnace solutionizing, quenching, natural aging, and artificial aging. Solutionizing is described as requiring at least 500°C for Mg and Si diffusion, with 577°C identified as the upper limit before liquidus. Quenching locks solutes into solid solution, with faster quenching generally producing greater strength but increasing deformation risk. AlSi10Mg has a relatively flat natural-aging response, but at least one hour of natural aging is reported to produce some hardness increase. The excerpt ends before providing the artificial-aging schedule or quantitative hardness/yield-strength results, so it cannot support a comparative table of direct-aging conditions and properties for the requested alloy families.

Other reported Scalmalloy® datasets show peak-aged yield strengths of about 453–520 MPa under treatments commonly centered on 598 K for 4 h or 623 K for 4 h. ## 2. mehta2023advancingnovelalmncrzr pages 1-3 (Context ID: pqac-00000047)

1. Introduction

High strength aluminium alloys are extremely sought after due to their exceptional speciﬁc
strength combined with general corrosion resistance and high recyclability potential. However,
there still exists several challenges in a wider adoption of aluminium alloys such as high
operating temperatures from currently available 473–493–573 K [1], [2]. To make mass
adoption possible, it is also important to avoid rare earth elements and critical elements such as
Sc, Ce etc. to these alloys. This is where novel processing routes can help achieve the goal of
pushing the material property envelope. Additive Manufacturing (AM) could provide the answer
to such needs. AM is a relatively new manufacturing technique involving layer by layer material
deposition in contrast to cast & wrought manufacturing route which have been around for long
[3], [4], [5]. Powder bed fusion-laser beam (PBF-LB) is a type of AM route which uses a focused
laser beam to selectively melt a small layer of powdered material (metal, polymer etc.), enabling
a high cooling rate of 103–105 K/s [5].
Since both the raw material used (metal powder) and the manufacturing of component (via PBF-
LB) involves high cooling rates, thus completely new alloys have been developed in the last few
years [6], [7], [8], [9]. The main aim has been to develop alloys which are suitable for the
process and do not create defects such as solidiﬁcation cracking. One way is to add elements
such as Ti, Zr via ex-situ or in-situ alloying to make the alloys printable. An example of ex-situ
alloying is nano functionalization techniques developed to coat Al-powder in order to cause
heterogeneous nucleation and make conventional grades of Aluminium alloys printable [8].
Another way has been to avoid cracking altogether and create alloys which are defect tolerant
[10], [11]. Some authors have leveraged both features together to create high strength
Aluminium alloys [6], [7], [12] reaching yield strengths as high as 500–550 MPa. When it
comes to designing high temperature strengths, entirely novel compositions such as Al-Ce-Mn
[13], Al-Fe-Cr [9] or Al-Mn-Ni-Cu-Zr [14] have been explored. These alloys reach > 150 MPa
yield strengths at temperatures of 573 K, which is quite promising. However, there are two
things lacking in the previously done works. The raw materials are fabricated with complex
techniques (such as nano functionalization [8]) when similar grain-reﬁnement results could be
achieved by relatively simpler direct alloying with Ti/Zr/Sc as shown by [6], [14], [15].
Additionally, by creating one-two alloy variants, the understanding of such novel alloy systems
are limited. Advanced characterisation combined with predicting strengthening of such alloy
systems deﬁnitely helps in understanding the role of the particular alloy, but it can miss the
complicated interactions between diﬀerent phases and elements present in the alloy. For
developing a better understanding of an alloy system such as ours (Al-Mn-Cr-Zr based), creating
several variants (ternary, quaternary and quinary) was deemed important.
In our previous work [16], [17] we have studied Al-Mn-Cr-Zr family of alloys by creating Al-
Mn-Cr, Al-Mn-Zr and Al-Mn-Cr-Zr as three variants, in order to explain the eﬀect of each
alloying element clearly. Additionally, it was shown that these alloys are agnostic to the process
and are defect tolerant. As-printed hardness > 100 HV combined with precipitation hardening
via direct ageing achieved peak hardness > 140 HV for these alloys [18]. Good mechanical
properties were observed with yield strength (YS) and ultimate tensile strength (UTS) close to
340 MPa and 440 MPa respectively [19]. However, these strength does not correspond to the
strongest aluminium alloys available (up to 500–550 MPa). The value creation aspect of this
alloy system would thus be enhanced if higher YS could be realised, combined with a higher
thermal stability as has been already shown before [20]. This study has shown to push the
boundaries of this alloy system to achieve the abovementioned objective. It has been done by
increasing the Zr content during atomisation beyond PBF-LB solubility limit and/or addition ofMg thus creating three new variants of the alloys. Zr increase caused grain reﬁnement and Mg
addition enhanced solid solution strength. These variants have been analysed using
characterization tools complemented with CALPHAD tools to understand the as-printed
microstructure-property relation. The resulting variants were then directly aged at 623 K and
648 K to benchmark against previously known best alloy. This comparison was conducted via
microhardness testing.
2. Materials and methods

2.1. Powder

Pre-alloyed spherical powder for this study was fabricated by gas atomization and provided by
Höganäs AB, Sweden in particle size distribution of 20–53 µm. Table 1 summarises the chemical
compositions of all alloys studied in their as-printed condition based on ICP-OES values
conducted at Höganäs AB, Sweden. The trace elements such as O were measured by combustion
gas analysis using LECO ON836 and CS844 instruments at Höganäs AB, Sweden. Alloy C from
the previous batch of alloys studied before [16] was chosen as a reference alloy for
benchmarking purpose.

impurities from the atomisation process.

2.2. PBF-LB processing

All alloys were processed in an EOS M290 machine with 100 µm spot size and 400 W (370 W
nominal power) Yb-ﬁber laser. A full factorial design of experiments (DOE) approach as shown
previously [16] was conducted on alloy C and alloy D by varying laser power between 200 and
370 W and laser scan speed between 375 and 2000 mm/s. The optimised processing parameters
were chosen as 370 W power, 0.13 mm hatch distance, 1300 mm/s laser speed and 0.03 mm
layer thickness with a scan rotation of 67° between each layer. It was seen that > 99.7 %
relative bulk density was observed for all four alloys at this parameter, as further outlined in the
results section. This set of parameters was then used to print cubes for all the alloys for
microstructure analysis. The cube samples were dimensioned 10 mm each side with a notch to
mark gas ﬂow direction, as elucidated in Fig. 1. After printing, the samples were cut with a cold
saw from the build plate.
2.3. Simulation software, microstructure evaluation and mechanical testing

All thermodynamics simulations were run using ThermoCalc 2022a software with TCAL8,
MOBAL6 databases. The alloy compositions for the simulation were assumed as the ones
received from ICP-AES values, and it was supposed that all elements are in solid solution in as-printed state. The samples were cut close to the centre of XZ plane at about 3–4 mm from centre
of top plane as shown in Fig. 1 followed by mounting in epoxy-based conductive thermoset
resin. The samples were prepared using a Streurs TegraPol 31 machine. The grinding/polishing
procedure is explained before [18], which includes grinding with silica grits up to 4000,
followed by polishing with 1 µm diamond suspension. A ﬁnal polishing step for SEM sample
preparation was conducted with OP-S silica suspension on a Streurs TegraPol 31 machine. Light
optical microscopy was done on a ZEISS Axioscope 7 machine with an automated scale enabling
the stitching of images to cover large cross sections. These large cross sections (40–50 mm2 per
sample) were measured at 10X objective to calculate relative density of each sample via image
analysis. Image J was used for image analysis. Microstructural evaluation was also done using a
Zeiss Gemini 450 SEM equipped with ﬁeld emission gun source equipped with a six channel
back scattered detector. Imaging was done with back scattered electron (BSE). The SEM is ﬁtted
with a ULTIM MAX Energy Dispersive X-ray Spectroscopy (EDS) detector from Oxford
Instruments, which enabled elemental mapping of microstructure at sub-micron resolutions. For
feature analysis done in the Gemini 450 SEM, beam voltage of 5 kV with 1 nA of probe current
was chosen with a 30 nm spatial resolution at 5kX magniﬁcation to study morphology of
precipitates in some of the selected materials. Two random areas of 150 µm × 150 µm each
were scanned along build direction (XZ plane) in each alloy. The stitching of images and initial
analysis was always conducted in the SEM itself using Aztec software from Oxford Instruments.

## pqac-00000049

From text 'martucci2023developmentandcharacterisation pages 20-21'.

A Martucci. Development and characterisation of al-based alloys processed by pbf-lb/m. Unknown journal, 2023.

The excerpt identifies design-of-experiments (DOE) using small cubic samples as the conventional method for LPBF/PBF-LB/M parameter optimization, typically targeting densification. However, because the process involves more than 50 parameters and each powder–machine combination requires optimization, full-factorial or broad bulk-sample DOE can consume substantial time and powder—an important limitation when only 100–300 g is available. Volumetric energy density (VED), calculated from laser power, scan speed, hatch distance, and layer thickness, is commonly used to reduce the parameter space, but it should not be treated as the sole design variable: equal VED values can produce different outcomes when power and speed differ. A more powder-efficient strategy is staged experimentation. {"artifact_type": "table", "description": "Create a comprehensive starting parameter recommendation table for 9 aluminum alloy families on an Aconity MIDI LPBF machine with ~80 um spot size, 20-63 um powder, 30-50 um layers. Columns: Alloy Family | Layer (um) | Power (W) | Speed (mm/s) | Hatch (um) | VED (J/mm3) | Plate T (°C) | Expected Density (%) | Main Failure Mode | Direct Aging Schedule | Key References. 

Row data based on gathered evidence:
1. AlSi10Mg: 30um, 350-370W, 1300-1650mm/s, 120-130um, 50-70 J/mm3, RT or 100°C, >99.5%, gas porosity/keyhole, 170°C/6h or T6, Leis 2021/Cauwenbergh 2021
2. Scalmalloy Al-Mg-Sc-Zr: 30um, 370W, 1000mm/s, 100um, ~123 J/mm3, 200°C beneficial, >99.5%, Mg evaporation/LoF, 325°C/4h, Schimback 2022/2024 on Aconity MIDI
3. Al-Mn-Cr-Zr / Al-Mn-Ti-Zr: 30um, 170-380W, 1000-1900mm/s, 100um, ~37-67 J/mm3, RT, ~99.5%, inherently crack-free/LoF, 350-375°C/14-24h, Mehta 2022/Mair 2022 
4. Al-Mg-Zr Addalloy-type: 30um, 350W, 1000mm/s, 130um, ~90 J/mm3, RT, >99%, Mg evaporation/LoF, 400°C/8h, Croteau/Belelli 2022
5. Al-Fe-Zr (Aheadd CP1) / Al-Fe-Mg-Zr: 30-60um, 370W, 1400mm/s, 130um, ~40-68 J/mm3, 100°C, >99.7%, gas porosity, 400°C/4h, Pauzon 2022/Li 2025
6. High-Mg Al-Mg-Si eutectic: 30um, 300-370W, 800-1300mm/s, 100-130um, ~60-100 J/mm3, 200-500°C needed if Mg>5wt%, >99% with grain refiners, cracking, needs grain refinement
7. Al-Mg-Er-Zr: 30um, 350W, 1000mm/s, 130um, ~90 J/mm3, RT, >99.5% (with sufficient Zr>1wt%), cracking if Er/Zr low, 325-375°C/3-8h, Guo 2022
8. 7xxx/2xxx Zr-modified: 30um, 300-370W, 800-1300mm/s, 100-130um, 50-80 J/mm3, 200-500°C, <99% without grain refiners, hot cracking, T6 after printing
9. Al-Ce / Al-Ni eutectic: 30-45um, 200-365W, 800-1500mm/s, 100um, 40-80 J/mm3, RT, >99.5%, inherently crack-free, limited aging response, Hesselmann 2022"}

function.arguments:
{"artifact_type": "table", "description": "Create a build-plate heating effects summary table for the 9 aluminum alloy families. Columns: Alloy Family | No Preheat (25°C) | 100-200°C | 300-500°C | Best Plate T | Net Assessment (Needs/Indifferent/Harmed). Based on gathered evidence:

1. AlSi10Mg: 25C fine, high strength; 200C stress relief but Si coarsening reduces strength, ductility similar; 300-500C excessive coarsening, overaging. Best: 25-100C. Indifferent to mild preheat.
2. Scalmalloy: 25C fine; 200C beneficial for in-situ cluster formation, improved as-built strength. Best: 200C. Benefits from preheat.
3. Al-Mn-Cr-Zr: 25C full supersaturation; preheat risks Mn/Cr supersaturation loss. Best: RT. Harmed by preheat.
4. Al-Mg-Zr Addalloy: 25C good; moderate preheat provides stress relief. Best: 25-100C. Indifferent.
5. Al-Fe-Zr CP1: 100C baseline; no strong need for higher. Best: 100C. Indifferent.
6. High-Mg Al-Mg-Si: 25C severe cracking; 200C reduces cracks somewhat; 500C needed for crack-free in 6182. Needs 500C preheat.
7. Al-Mg-Er-Zr: Similar to Scalmalloy, 25C fine; 200C may benefit precipitation. Best: 25-100C. Indifferent.
8. 7xxx/2xxx: 25C cracked; 100-200C still cracked; 400C changes crack morphology but doesn't eliminate; 500C may help with grain refiners. Needs preheat + grain refiners.
9. Al-Ce/Al-Ni: 25C fine, inherently crack-free. Best: RT. Indifferent."}

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition
        - InterventionName (0.8): Primary intervention name
        - OverallStatus: Trial status

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):
        - InterventionOtherName (0.75): Alternative intervention names
        - Phase (0.65): Trial phase
        - StdAge (0.65): Standard age groups
        - Keyword (0.6): Study keywords
        - BriefSummary (0.6): Short description
        - SecondaryOutcomeMeasure (0.5): Secondary outcomes

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)
        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

Supported Enums:
    Phase:
        - EARLY_PHASE1: Early Phase 1
        - PHASE1: Phase 1
        - PHASE2: Phase 2
        - PHASE3: Phase 3
        - PHASE4: Phase 4
        - NA: Not Applicable

    StandardAge:
        - CHILD: Child
        - ADULT: Adult
        - OLDER_ADULT: Older Adult

    Status:
        - RECRUITING: Currently recruiting participants
        - ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING: Active but not recruiting
        - COMPLETED: Study completed
        - ENROLLING_BY_INVITATION: Enrolling by invitation only
        - NOT_YET_RECRUITING: Not yet recruiting
        - SUSPENDED: Study suspended
        - TERMINATED: Study terminated
        - WITHDRAWN: Study withdrawn
        - AVAILABLE: Available

        - TEMPORARILY_NOT_AVAILABLE: Temporarily not available
        - APPROVED_FOR_MARKETING: Approved for marketing
        - WITHHELD: Withheld
        - UNKNOWN: Unknown status

    StudyType:
        - INTERVENTIONAL: Interventional studies
        - OBSERVATIONAL: Observational studies
        - EXPANDED_ACCESS: Expanded access studies

    PrimaryPurpose:
        - TREATMENT: Treatment
        - PREVENTION: Prevention
        - DIAGNOSTIC: Diagnostic
        - ECT: Educational/Counseling/Training
        - SUPPORTIVE_CARE: Supportive Care

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: read_text
info.description:
Given a list of text names, read their contents.

This tool is valuable to read the full contents of specific parts of documents,
complementing the `gather_evidence` tool's indirect approach.
This can be an especially useful tool if `gather_evidence` does not find evidence,
but you think it is very likely that specific documents are still relevant to the question.

text_name_list.description:
A list of up to 10 text names to read.
These text names can be any valid text names retrieved by other tools.
text_name_list.title: Text Name List

info.name: collect_cited_papers_in_evidence
info.description:
Collect papers by traversing the citations of relevant papers to increase the paper count.

This tool has no effect if called when paper count or relevant papers are zero.
This tool will find papers that are likely to lead to more relevant evidence.
The papers found have a higher chance of relevance because this tool starts from relevant evidence.
This tool's usefulness increases with the amount of gathered evidence as there's more citations to consider.

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)
query.title: Query

after.description:
Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.
after.title: After

before.description:
Maximum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20200101' for patents before Jan 1, 2020.
before.title: Before

date_type.description:
Type of date that after and before refer to. Must be either 'publication'
or 'filing'. Only necessary to set if after and/or before are set.
date_type.title: Date Type

inventor.description: Filter by inventor name(s). Comma-separated for multiple.
inventor.title: Inventor

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: update_plan
info.description:
Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

plan_objective_id.description: The id of the objective to update.
plan_objective_id.title: Plan Objective Id

updated_plan_objective_json.description:
A JSON string representing the updated objective.
It should be a dictionary with the with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id matching plan_objective_id, if not found, a new objective is created.
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
updated_plan_objective_json.title: Updated Plan Objective Json

info.name: open_targets_search
info.description:
Search for disease-target associations from OpenTargets database.

Adds new disease-target association data to the state and returns top search results.

disease_names.description:
List of disease names to search for.
Usage:
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->
    Returns top targets for Alzheimer's
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's", "Diabetes"], target_names = ["PSEN1"] ->
    Filters for only PSEN1-Alzheimer's/Diabetes evidence

List of target names to search for.
Usage:
target_names = ["BACE1"] ->
    Returns top diseases associated with BACE1
target_names = ["BACE1", "APP"], disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->
    Filters for only these target-Alzheimer's pairs
target_names = ["BACE1"], drug_names = ["Aducanumab"] ->
    Filters for BACE1 disease pairs treated by Aducanumab

List of drug names to generate or filter results.
Usage:
drug_names = ["Aducanumab"] ->
    Returns all disease-target pairs treated by Aducanumab
drug_names = ["Aducanumab"], disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->

drug_names = ["Aducanumab"], target_names = ["BACE1"] ->
    Filters for BACE1 disease pairs treated by Aducanumab

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string encoding an object with an "objectives" list;
never pass objectives separately.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
plan_json.title: Plan Json

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?
   - Are you extracting from the right context (not noise like page numbers)?

4. Sanity Check: Read your answer. Does it directly address what was asked?

Don't use Markdown image syntax like ![...](...) to reference media in your answer,
because media get automatically linked by the system based on your answer's citations.

Write in the style of a scientific article, with concise sentences and
coherent paragraphs. This answer will be used directly,
so do not add any extraneous information.

messages.content:
Use the tools to answer the question: We will print nine different aluminium alloys, each as single tracks, density cubes and sub-size tensile bars, on an Aconity MIDI laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) machine (single-mode fibre laser, 400 W class with up to 1 kW optional, spot about 80 um, argon, build-plate heating available; a high-temperature heating module may reach 500 C or more). Powder is ultrasonically atomized in-house, sieved to about 20-63 um (D50 about 45-55 um), 100-300 g per alloy, so layers of 30-50 um and a reduced build platform. Please review the literature and give starting process windows and what build-plate heating does, per alloy family, quantitatively.

Alloy families: (1) AlSi10Mg; (2) Scalmalloy-type Al-Mg-Sc-Zr; (3) Al-Mn-Cr-Zr and Al-Mn-Ti-Zr; (4) Al-Mg-Zr (Addalloy-type); (5) Al-Fe-Zr (Aheadd CP1-type) and Al-Fe-Mg-Zr; (6) high-Mg Al-Mg-Si(-Mn) eutectic-type; (7) Al-Mg-Er-Zr; (8) Zr-modified 7xxx (Al-Zn-Mg-Cu-Zr) and 2xxx; (9) Al-Ce and Al-Ni eutectic alloys.

1. Published parameter sets on Aconity machines (MIDI, MIDI+, MINI, LAB, TWO) for aluminium alloys: laser power, scan speed, hatch, layer thickness, spot size, scan strategy, preheat, gas flow, resulting density. Include AlSi10Mg, Scalmalloy, 6061, 7075, 2024, Al-Mn-Sc, Al-Ce and any novel alloys. Which universities run Al on Aconity machines?
2. For each family above: the published crack-free, >99.5 % dense windows on any 200-400 W machine with a 70-100 um spot (power, speed, hatch, layer, volumetric energy density, plate temperature), and how the window shifts for 50 um layers and coarser powder.
3. Build-plate heating: for each family, the measured effect of 25 C vs 100-200 C vs 300-500 C plate temperature on (a) solidification and liquation cracking, (b) density and hydrogen porosity, (c) residual stress and distortion, (d) as-built strength (in-situ ageing or over-ageing: Si network coarsening in AlSi10Mg, Al3(Sc,Zr) precipitation in Scalmalloy at 200 C, Mn/Cr/Zr supersaturation loss), (e) Mg and Zn evaporation, (f) powder caking / sintering and reuse. Which families need a heated plate, which are indifferent, and which are harmed? Give the best plate temperature for each. Include the 6061 at 500 C result (Uddin et al.) and similar high-preheat studies for 7075 and 2024.
4. How to set a first print window for an alloy nobody has printed: normalized-enthalpy and keyhole-threshold criteria, lack-of-fusion criteria from melt-pool width/depth, Eagar-Tsai / Rosenthal estimates and their accuracy for Al (absorptivity values to use for Al alloys with powder, about 0.2-0.6 depending on mode), balling / humping limits at high speed, and how alloy thermal conductivity (e.g. Mn/Cr/Fe-rich alloys with low conductivity versus high-conductivity dilute alloys) and Mg/Zn vapour pressure move the window.
5. Efficient experimental designs when powder is scarce (100-300 g per alloy): single tracks on bare plate or on a thin powder layer, number of tracks per composition, small cubes (5-10 mm), mini tensile geometries (ASTM E8 sub-size, SS-J3, miniature dog-bones) and how their strength and elongation compare with full-size bars; reduced build-volume inserts; multi-material / multi-powder plates; in-situ alloying shortcuts. What is the minimum powder to get density + hardness + three tensile values?
6. Scan strategy and other settings that matter for novel Al alloys: 67 degree rotation, stripes vs chessboard, remelting, contour scans, oxygen level in the chamber (below 100-500 ppm), gas flow, recoater type for coarser / less flowable powder, powder drying (humidity; hydrogen porosity), and the effect of oxygen content of the powder.
7. Direct-ageing schedules after printing for each family and expected hardness / yield response; whether to stress relieve.
8. A recommended starting table for the nine families on an Aconity MIDI with a 20-63 um powder: layer thickness, power, speed, hatch, plate temperature, expected melt-pool depth/width, expected density, main failure mode to watch for, and a compact 12-20 condition design of experiments around that centre.

Give DOIs. Separate measured data from extrapolation.

Start by making a plan, and update the plan as you go. Your answer will be returned to the user when all plan objectives are completed. Be thorough and ensure your evidence matches the user's question.
I'll start by creating a comprehensive plan to address this multi-faceted question about LPBF processing of aluminum alloys on an Aconity MIDI machine.

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Thin-walled plate lattice structures fabricated from AlSi10Mg via laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) promise exceptional stiffness-to-weight ratios for lightweight applications. However, wall thicknesses below
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:tex-math>$$\sim {500}{\upmu }{\textrm{m}}$$</jats:tex-math>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    commonly introduce geometric variations, surface roughness, porosity, and strong crystallographic texture, which degrade mechanical performance. This study investigates a stretching-dominated anisotropic plate lattice structure with
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:tex-math>$${200}{\upmu }{\textrm{m}}$$</jats:tex-math>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    walls, derived from a 2.5D honeycomb topology and optimized for uniaxial and multiaxial loadings. Overhang-free design of this structure enhances reproducibility and dimensional accuracy. An additional advantage of the parallel continuous plates is that they enable direct analytical calculation of effective mechanical properties via rule of mixtures. An adapted single-laser-track exposure strategy (wall thickness-to-spot size ratio
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:tex-math>$$\sim {1.25}$$</jats:tex-math>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    ) suppresses downsizing effects, producing a homogeneous microstructure with a fine, intact eutectic cellular network free of coarsened Si regions. Measured–simulated deviations stay in the single-digit percentage range: normalized by relative density (
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:tex-math>$$\rho ^*$$</jats:tex-math>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    ) axial Young’s modulus and yield strength closely match literature values for dense, peak-aged LPBF AlSi10Mg, while transverse values reach
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:tex-math>$$\sim {30}{\textrm{GPa}}$$</jats:tex-math>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    and
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:tex-math>$$\sim {117}{\textrm{MPa}}$$</jats:tex-math>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    (
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:tex-math>$$\rho ^*={0.267}$$</jats:tex-math>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    ), respectively. Finite element models incorporating CT-derived geometry of a lattice cell and EBSD-based orientation data show that texture reduces axial Young’s modulus by up to
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:tex-math>$$\sim {5.5}\%$$</jats:tex-math>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    . While intra-cell geometric fluctuations contribute
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:tex-math>$$\le {2}\%$$</jats:tex-math>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    to the normalized Young’s modulus, inter-cell variations can introduce
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:tex-math>$$\sim {10}\%$$</jats:tex-math>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    scatter of absolute stiffness, which dominates the residual sample-to-sample differences. Strategic fillets at plate intersections enhance overall lightweight efficiency of this anisotropic metamaterial by improving transverse specific stiffness and elongation at break.
                  </jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>Abstract. Multimaterial additive manufacturing enables the fabrication of components that integrate materials with distinct properties, unlocking unprecedented opportunities for the optimization of functionally integrated mechanical parts. Combined with the design flexibility of additive manufacturing, this capability allows for the creation of innovative solutions tailored to specific performance requirements. A novel platform for multimaterial Powder Bed Fusion – Laser Melting (PBF-LM) has been recently presented with the aim of depositing up to three materials on the same layer to achieve multimaterial products. Despite its unprecedented potential, multimaterial LPBF brings several challenges to achieve high-quality components without flaws or defects. This study leverages real-time process monitoring to aid process parameter optimization for multimaterial LPBF, with a special focus on combining steel and copper alloys for space and energy applications.</jats:p>
