It describes Rosenthal’s moving point-source model, with temperature expressed using absorbed power (𝑛Q), thermal conductivity, diffusivity, scan velocity, and distance from the heat source. The model is appropriate when the beam radius is much smaller than the thermal diffusion distance, 𝑟b ≪ 𝑟o, where 𝑟o = √(4αte); it is particularly applicable to high-conductivity materials. The excerpt also gives a one-dimensional analytical model for a stationary, infinitely large beam, valid in the opposite regime, 𝑟b ≫ 𝑟o, and notes that melt-pool depth is obtained by solving for the position where temperature reaches the melting temperature. Powder absorptivity is modeled from bulk absorptivity: 𝑛 = m𝑛s, with multiplicity factor m fitted as 1.0383𝑛s^−0.487. Temperature dependence and changes upon melting are explicitly neglected. Process-window density is linked to melt-pool overlap: the dimensionless overlap depth 𝑑* = 𝑑int/l, with 𝑑* ≥ 1 theoretically indicating complete overlap under ideal conditions. contexts.context: The excerpt discusses analytical and experimentally assisted approaches for predicting melt-pool dimensions, densification, and process windows in PBF-LB/M, but it does not provide a normalized-enthalpy equation or explicit Eagar–Tsai/Rosenthal formulations. It notes that Letenneur et al. used an analytical thermal-field model to predict melt-pool dimensions and experimentally correlated those predictions with final-part density, thereby linking process parameters to densification. The model was simplified because it did not include heat exchange and powder-spreading conditions. For aluminum alloys, absorptivity is strongly dependent on material condition, powder surface roughness, and laser wavelength; shorter wavelengths generally produce higher absorption. Aluminum has low absorption and high reflectivity at the conventional YAG wavelength, often motivating high volumetric energy density values. The excerpt reports that green-laser processing increased aluminum absorption by more than twofold relative to YAG, but gives no numerical absorptivity values. For the conduction-to-keyhole transition, Patel et al.’s criterion is summarized as surface vaporization and a vaporization depth greater than 0.5 times the beam radius, respectively, marking the transition thresholds. The applicability of this criterion is less robust for aluminum because of high reflectivity, high thermal conductivity, and volatile alloying elements such as magnesium.

contexts.context: Compared with the approximately unheated 35°C build plate, preheating the AlSi10Mg LPBF platform to 200°C substantially changes the thermal history and coarsens the microstructure. The α-Al cellular structure and Si-rich precipitates become larger, while the Si-rich eutectic network becomes thicker and less interconnected. This coarsened, less interconnected Si network provides a lower strengthening effect and is more susceptible to damage. Consequently, tensile strength decreases at 200°C relative to 35°C, although the fracture strain (ductility) remains similar rather than improving. The principal benefit of 200°C preheating is thermal-stress relief: residual stress becomes negligible, whereas the 35°C condition is associated with tensile residual stresses of approximately 50 MPa. The supplied excerpt does not provide comparative density or porosity results, so no supported conclusion about how 200°C preheating affects density can be drawn from these pages. It does note that prior fatigue-focused work considered porosity, but the excerpt does not report a density change attributable to preheating.

In that comparison, preheating increases as-built yield strength and work hardening, while reducing ductility; ultimate tensile strength is approximately similar because the ambient and preheated materials have comparable tensile strength. The preheated material has greater measured porosity (1.7% versus 0.9%), implying lower relative density, and this porosity difference is identified as the likely main cause of reduced elongation. Eutectic fraction (about 16.7–16.8%), cellular size (590 versus 520 nm), and grain size show no major differences, so the excerpt provides no evidence of substantial Si-network coarsening from the platform-temperature change. contexts.context: The excerpt establishes that increasing the LPBF build-platform temperature from 35°C to 200°C changes the thermal gradient and therefore the AlSi10Mg microstructure. The Si-rich eutectic phase forms an interconnected network in the fine and coarse melt-pool zones, and this network contributes to strengthening by carrying load and hindering dislocation motion. Thermal input is expected to coarsen and globularise this network, reducing its strengthening effect and thereby weakening the material. In the reported comparison, the mean melt-pool size was broadly similar at 35°C and 200°C, but the heat-affected zone and coarse melt-pool zone were each approximately twice as thick at 200°C, producing a melt-pool border of double thickness. The excerpt does not provide the quantitative results needed to determine the full effects of 200°C preheating on Si-network coarsening, tensile strength, ductility, residual stress, or density. It also does not state direct residual-stress or density comparisons. Thus, it supports an expected coarsening/weakening trend and a clear change in melt-pool substructure, but not definitive numerical conclusions for all properties asked about.

contexts.question:
We will print nine different aluminium alloys, each as single tracks, density cubes and sub-size tensile bars, on an Aconity MIDI laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) machine (single-mode fibre laser, 400 W class with up to 1 kW optional, spot about 80 um, argon, build-plate heating available; a high-temperature heating module may reach 500 C or more). Powder is ultrasonically atomized in-house, sieved to about 20-63 um (D50 about 45-55 um), 100-300 g per alloy, so layers of 30-50 um and a reduced build platform. Please review the literature and give starting process windows and what build-plate heating does, per alloy family, quantitatively.

Alloy families: (1) AlSi10Mg; (2) Scalmalloy-type Al-Mg-Sc-Zr; (3) Al-Mn-Cr-Zr and Al-Mn-Ti-Zr; (4) Al-Mg-Zr (Addalloy-type); (5) Al-Fe-Zr (Aheadd CP1-type) and Al-Fe-Mg-Zr; (6) high-Mg Al-Mg-Si(-Mn) eutectic-type; (7) Al-Mg-Er-Zr; (8) Zr-modified 7xxx (Al-Zn-Mg-Cu-Zr) and 2xxx; (9) Al-Ce and Al-Ni eutectic alloys.

1. Published parameter sets on Aconity machines (MIDI, MIDI+, MINI, LAB, TWO) for aluminium alloys: laser power, scan speed, hatch, layer thickness, spot size, scan strategy, preheat, gas flow, resulting density. Include AlSi10Mg, Scalmalloy, 6061, 7075, 2024, Al-Mn-Sc, Al-Ce and any novel alloys. Which universities run Al on Aconity machines?
2. For each family above: the published crack-free, >99.5 % dense windows on any 200-400 W machine with a 70-100 um spot (power, speed, hatch, layer, volumetric energy density, plate temperature), and how the window shifts for 50 um layers and coarser powder.
3. Build-plate heating: for each family, the measured effect of 25 C vs 100-200 C vs 300-500 C plate temperature on (a) solidification and liquation cracking, (b) density and hydrogen porosity, (c) residual stress and distortion, (d) as-built strength (in-situ ageing or over-ageing: Si network coarsening in AlSi10Mg, Al3(Sc,Zr) precipitation in Scalmalloy at 200 C, Mn/Cr/Zr supersaturation loss), (e) Mg and Zn evaporation, (f) powder caking / sintering and reuse. Which families need a heated plate, which are indifferent, and which are harmed? Give the best plate temperature for each. Include the 6061 at 500 C result (Uddin et al.) and similar high-preheat studies for 7075 and 2024.
4. How to set a first print window for an alloy nobody has printed: normalized-enthalpy and keyhole-threshold criteria, lack-of-fusion criteria from melt-pool width/depth, Eagar-Tsai / Rosenthal estimates and their accuracy for Al (absorptivity values to use for Al alloys with powder, about 0.2-0.6 depending on mode), balling / humping limits at high speed, and how alloy thermal conductivity (e.g. Mn/Cr/Fe-rich alloys with low conductivity versus high-conductivity dilute alloys) and Mg/Zn vapour pressure move the window.
5. Efficient experimental designs when powder is scarce (100-300 g per alloy): single tracks on bare plate or on a thin powder layer, number of tracks per composition, small cubes (5-10 mm), mini tensile geometries (ASTM E8 sub-size, SS-J3, miniature dog-bones) and how their strength and elongation compare with full-size bars; reduced build-volume inserts; multi-material / multi-powder plates; in-situ alloying shortcuts. What is the minimum powder to get density + hardness + three tensile values?
6. Scan strategy and other settings that matter for novel Al alloys: 67 degree rotation, stripes vs chessboard, remelting, contour scans, oxygen level in the chamber (below 100-500 ppm), gas flow, recoater type for coarser / less flowable powder, powder drying (humidity; hydrogen porosity), and the effect of oxygen content of the powder.
7. Direct-ageing schedules after printing for each family and expected hardness / yield response; whether to stress relieve.
8. A recommended starting table for the nine families on an Aconity MIDI with a 20-63 um powder: layer thickness, power, speed, hatch, plate temperature, expected melt-pool depth/width, expected density, main failure mode to watch for, and a compact 12-20 condition design of experiments around that centre.

Give DOIs. Separate measured data from extrapolation.

contexts.context: The excerpt focuses on rapidly solidified Al–Mn–Cr–Zr alloys for PBF-LB. Literature suggests ~5.8 wt% Mn+Cr could provide ~300 MPa solid-solution strengthening, versus ~100 MPa for equivalent Mg. Al–5Mn–2.5Cr reportedly retains hardness to 523 K and may precipitation-strengthen during direct ageing at 573–673 K through semi-coherent Al₁₂(Mn,Cr); Zr may form nanometric Al₃Zr during ageing around 623–723 K, adding up to 30–35 HV. contexts.context: Schimbäck et al. (Materials & Design 224 (2022) 111410) studied Scalmalloy on an Aconity MIDI at Innsbruck, using gas-atomized powder (d10 27.3, d50 42.6, d90 64.7 μm; Mg 4.50, Sc 0.73, Zr 0.27 wt%; O 0.03%). The machine had a 1000 W Yb:YAG laser and resistive build-platform heating to 800 °C. Their normalized enthalpy was \(ΔH=P/(v_s\sqrt{r_L^3})\). Increasing \(ΔH\) increased penetration and shifted conduction (HC) toward keyhole (KH) welding; KH produced keyhole porosity and up to 1.2 wt% Mg burn-off, versus 0.3% in HC. Large spatter caused lack-of-fusion pores.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not provide a dedicated quantitative dataset for Al-Mg-Er-Zr alloys, nor does it list their laser power, scan speed, hatch distance, layer thickness, density, or as-built versus aged mechanical properties. It gives general LPBF guidance: approximately 60 J/mm³ was identified as a critical energy density for minimizing porosity, while 60–75 J/mm³ was reported as the multiple-layer threshold for maximum densification. Increasing scan speed lowers energy density and can promote lack-of-fusion porosity; excessive energy density can instead produce keyhole porosity. The passage discusses grain refinement through control of temperature gradient and growth rate, particularly by adjusting laser power and scan speed. It also notes that heat treatment can affect grain size and properties, and that HIP closes internal voids and reduces residual stress. The closest alloy-related result is Scalmalloy®, which achieved 520 MPa yield strength and 530 MPa ultimate tensile strength after treatment at 325°C for 4 hours, attributed to Al3(Sc,Zr) precipitation; this is not an Al-Mg-Er-Zr result and should not be treated as directly equivalent. The displayed table includes some AlSi10Mg parameters and properties, but not the requested alloy.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides direct-aging information for an LPBF Al-Mg-Zr-Sc alloy with reduced Sc content, which may be relevant as a Sc-containing comparison but is not a complete dataset for all alloys listed in the question. Aging treatments were investigated at 300, 350, 375, and 400 °C. The strongest explicitly reported response was aging at 350 °C for 24 h, which increased hardness from 105 HV in the as-built condition to 160 HV. At 375 and 400 °C, comparable peak hardness of approximately 155 HV was reached after 8 h. The excerpt does not report the corresponding yield strengths, nor does it provide direct-aging schedules or resulting properties for AlSi10Mg, conventional Scalmalloy, Al-Mn-Cr-Zr, Al-Fe-Zr, or Al-Ce alloys. Mechanistically, the hardness increase is associated with precipitation of continuous and discontinuous L12-Al3(Sc,Zr) particles. Simulations predicted Al3(Sc,Zr) precipitation during aging and no secondary Al3Zr precipitates under the modeled conditions. The study also describes a four-stage precipitation sequence—nucleation, growth, transition, and coarsening—and indicates that lower supersaturation promotes earlier coarsening. Therefore, the supplied excerpt supports only the Al-Mg-Zr-Sc hardness schedule; additional alloy-specific literature is needed to establish comparable temperature/time treatments and yield strengths for the other alloy systems.

For AlSi10Mg, the commonly cited stress-relief treatment is 300°C for 2 hours; lower treatments of 240–250°C reportedly increase ductility while producing little or no visible microstructural change, although the extent of residual-stress reduction remains unverified. The conventional precipitation-hardening route consists of stress relief, furnace solutionizing, quenching, natural aging, and artificial aging. Solutionizing is described as requiring at least 500°C for Mg and Si diffusion, with 577°C identified as the upper limit before liquidus. Quenching locks solutes into solid solution, with faster quenching generally producing greater strength but increasing deformation risk. AlSi10Mg has a relatively flat natural-aging response, but at least one hour of natural aging is reported to produce some hardness increase. The excerpt ends before providing the artificial-aging schedule or quantitative hardness/yield-strength results, so it cannot support a comparative table of direct-aging conditions and properties for the requested alloy families.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides direct-aging information only for the LPBF Al-Mg-Sc-Zr alloy Scalmalloy®, not for AlSi10Mg, Al-Mn-Cr-Zr, Al-Fe-Zr, or Al-Ce alloys. For Scalmalloy®, the study identifies 598 K (325 °C) for 4 h as the selected peak-hardness treatment. It also reports that 573 K (300 °C) for 8 h can produce a peak-hardening response, while literature values include aging between 573 and 623 K for 4–12 h, and a two-step treatment of 573 K for 3 h plus 633 K for 4 h. At 623 K (350 °C), hardening begins rapidly, with peak hardness reached within 30 min, followed by deterioration with longer aging. The supplied pages do not state the numerical hardness value corresponding to these treatments. For the alloy studied in this work, the peak-aged tensile properties are approximately 468 MPa yield strength (Rp0.2), 517 MPa ultimate tensile strength, and 8.5% reduction in area, using 598 K for 4 h. Other reported Scalmalloy® datasets show peak-aged yield strengths of about 453–520 MPa under treatments commonly centered on 598 K for 4 h or 623 K for 4 h. Therefore, this excerpt supports a Scalmalloy schedule and yield-strength range, but not comparable data for the other requested alloy families.

contexts.context: Mehta, Frisk and Nyborg (Chalmers, 2022; DOI: **10.1016/j.jallcom.2022.165870**) studied novel Al–Mn–Cr–Zr alloys for PBF-LB. The alloys were reported crack-free, with as-printed supersaturation approximately **three times equilibrium solubility** and **102 HV** hardness. Direct ageing produced Al–Mn and Al–Zr precipitates, including Al₁₂Mn and Al₃Zr; grain-boundary precipitation preceded bulk precipitation. Peak hardness reached **143 HV at 623 K (350 °C) for 24 h** or **142 HV at 648 K (375 °C) for 14 h**. The excerpt does not provide machine parameters, plate heating, density, or tensile data.

Please review the literature and give starting process windows and what build-plate heating does, per alloy family, quantitatively.

Alloy families: (1) AlSi10Mg; (2) Scalmalloy-type Al-Mg-Sc-Zr; (3) Al-Mn-Cr-Zr and Al-Mn-Ti-Zr; (4) Al-Mg-Zr (Addalloy-type); (5) Al-Fe-Zr (Aheadd CP1-type) and Al-Fe-Mg-Zr; (6) high-Mg Al-Mg-Si(-Mn) eutectic-type; (7) Al-Mg-Er-Zr; (8) Zr-modified 7xxx (Al-Zn-Mg-Cu-Zr) and 2xxx; (9) Al-Ce and Al-Ni eutectic alloys.

1. Published parameter sets on Aconity machines (MIDI, MIDI+, MINI, LAB, TWO) for aluminium alloys: laser power, scan speed, hatch, layer thickness, spot size, scan strategy, preheat, gas flow, resulting density. Include AlSi10Mg, Scalmalloy, 6061, 7075, 2024, Al-Mn-Sc, Al-Ce and any novel alloys. Which universities run Al on Aconity machines?
2. For each family above: the published crack-free, >99.5 % dense windows on any 200-400 W machine with a 70-100 um spot (power, speed, hatch, layer, volumetric energy density, plate temperature), and how the window shifts for 50 um layers and coarser powder.
3. Build-plate heating: for each family, the measured effect of 25 C vs 100-200 C vs 300-500 C plate temperature on (a) solidification and liquation cracking, (b) density and hydrogen porosity, (c) residual stress and distortion, (d) as-built strength (in-situ ageing or over-ageing: Si network coarsening in AlSi10Mg, Al3(Sc,Zr) precipitation in Scalmalloy at 200 C, Mn/Cr/Zr supersaturation loss), (e) Mg and Zn evaporation, (f) powder caking / sintering and reuse. Which families need a heated plate, which are indifferent, and which are harmed? Give the best plate temperature for each. Include the 6061 at 500 C result (Uddin et al.) and similar high-preheat studies for 7075 and 2024.

A recommended starting table for the nine families on an Aconity MIDI with a 20-63 um powder: layer thickness, power, speed, hatch, plate temperature, expected melt-pool depth/width, expected density, main failure mode to watch for, and a compact 12-20 condition design of experiments around that centre.

Give DOIs. Separate measured data from extrapolation.

contexts.context: Leis, Weber, and Graf (University of Stuttgart) studied AlSi10Mg LPBF over 10.8–1754 W, 35–200 µm beams, and 0.7–1.3 m/s. They identified simple heating, heat-conduction melting (HCM), key-bowl melting (KBM), and deep-penetration melting (DPM). The low-porosity, efficient window was \(P_L/d_b=2000\)–5200 W/mm, centered at 3000–3500 W/mm (KBM), with 7–8% efficiency. Below 2000 W/mm caused balling/lack of fusion; above 5200 W/mm produced <5% efficiency and >10% pores. DOI: **10.3390/ma14185255**.

contexts.context: Li et al. (University of Groningen; Central South University) report a novel LPBF Al–Fe–Mg–Zr eutectic alloy. It was “crack-free” with 99.8% relative density, ultrafine grains, and cellular-lamellar microstructure. Direct aging at 400°C for 4 h increased YS to 376.1 MPa (+72.6%) and UTS to 405.8 MPa (+30.7%), while elongation fell to 11.1%. YS remained 124 MPa at 350°C; after 400°C/100 h, properties stayed strong, attributed to slow Al13Fe4 coarsening (0.98 nm³/s) and stable Al3Zr. DOI: 10.1080/17452759.2025.2516663.

contexts.context: The excerpt concerns LPBF Al–Mg–Mn–Er–Zr alloys, not Aconity parameters. Scalmalloy (Al–4.6Mg–0.66Sc–0.42Zr wt.%) reportedly exceeds 500 MPa with little build-orientation anisotropy after heat treatment (Spierings et al.). Addalloy (Al–3.66Mg–1.57Zr) remains below 400 MPa despite Al₃Zr precipitation. Three experimental compositions contained Mg 5.70–6.40%, Mn 0.40–0.81%, Er 0.40–1.10%, Zr 0.04–0.36%, oxygen 0.037–0.060%. Higher Er/Zr and refined equiaxed grains reduced cracking; specimen 3# was crack-free. Aging studied 200–550°C (3 h) and 325–375°C (125 h).

contexts.context: For alloy C (an Al–Mn–Zr-type alloy), microscopy found limited local grain refinement in the as-printed state, with precipitates at melt-pool boundaries. contexts.context: The excerpt directly supports using Design of Experiments (DoE) rather than one-variable-at-a-time testing for LPBF/PBF-LB/M parameter optimization. LPBF involves more than 50 variables, including laser energy, scan speed, spot diameter, focus position, hatch pattern, scan rotation, beam compensation, and hatch/contour sequence. Because powder and machine combinations require tailored parameter sets, exhaustive testing can be impractical, particularly when powder is limited. The text states that OVAT is inefficient for many factors and cannot adequately capture interactions between interconnected parameters. For a constrained experimental campaign using single tracks and small density cubes, the excerpt identifies screening designs such as fractional factorial and Plackett–Burman designs as potentially efficient ways to reduce the number of runs, followed by factorial or response-surface designs for modeling and refinement. Central Composite and Box–Behnken designs are specifically given as optimization approaches. The recommended DoE workflow consists of planning, screening, modeling, execution, analysis/optimization, and verification/validation. DoE can relate process parameters to outcomes, reduce defect rates and surface roughness, improve mechanical properties, and minimize material waste and energy consumption. However, the excerpt does not provide specific powder-saving quantities, specimen geometries, single-track protocols, or an explicit 100–300 g powder allocation strategy.
contexts.question: What are efficient experimental designs for LPBF parameter optimization with limited powder (100-300g)? Single track experiments, small density cubes, minimum powder consumption, design of experiments approaches for additive manufacturing?

contexts.context: The excerpt supports using statistically efficient DOE strategies for LPBF parameter optimization when powder is limited. Although it does not specifically discuss single-track tests, small density cubes, or a 100–300 g powder budget, it emphasizes minimizing experiments while maximizing information because powder and machine time are costly. Full factorial designs are straightforward and useful when prior information is limited, but they become inefficient as the number of factors or levels increases: three factors at three levels require 27 samples, and broad parameter ranges can yield low-resolution results. More economical alternatives include orthogonal arrays, fractional factorial designs, and Taguchi methods, typically analyzed using ANOVA and signal-to-noise ratios. The cited Ti6Al4V study obtained an optimal parameter combination with 16 samples using Taguchi methods. Regression-based response surface methodology (RSM) can also construct surrogate models and optimize several responses simultaneously; one Ti-6Al-4V example modeled surface roughness, porosity, elastic modulus, and compressive strength from three inputs using 17 samples. These approaches are relevant for organizing a staged LPBF study in which low-powder screening experiments identify promising power, scan-speed, hatch-spacing, or related parameter regions before more material-intensive validation.

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies design-of-experiments (DOE) using small cubic samples as the conventional method for LPBF/PBF-LB/M parameter optimization, typically targeting densification. However, because the process involves more than 50 parameters and each powder–machine combination requires optimization, full-factorial or broad bulk-sample DOE can consume substantial time and powder—an important limitation when only 100–300 g is available. Volumetric energy density (VED), calculated from laser power, scan speed, hatch distance, and layer thickness, is commonly used to reduce the parameter space, but it should not be treated as the sole design variable: equal VED values can produce different outcomes when power and speed differ. A more powder-efficient strategy is staged experimentation. First, use single-track experiments (SSTs) to rapidly screen many laser-power/scan-speed combinations using track width, continuity, and morphology. SST results can also support estimation of a suitable hatch distance through geometric overlap, reducing the number of bulk cubes required. Then validate the narrowed parameter window with a limited DOE of small density cubes, including relevant hatch-distance and layer-thickness levels. The excerpt cautions that SSTs cannot fully reproduce layer-by-layer effects, especially cracking in Al alloys, so bulk validation remains necessary. Layer thickness should also be experimentally considered because it strongly affects productivity, surface finish, densification, and mechanical performance.

contexts.context: The excerpt supports a staged, material-efficient experimental strategy for LPBF parameter studies, although it does not directly quantify powder consumption for 100–300 g inventories or specify small-cube geometries. It describes beginning with single-scan weld lines to build an experimental database for melt-pool-size prediction and to test commonly used process metrics such as energy density. The findings caution that energy density is applicable only within narrow process windows, so optimization should vary laser power and scan speed explicitly rather than relying on energy density alone. High-speed imaging of single tracks can additionally reveal melt-pool instability, bead formation, denudation, and interactions between entrained powder particles and the melt pool. For subsequent validation, square pillar samples were used to study solidification, with thermal gradient and solidification rate strongly dependent on laser power and scan speed. The work also used a design-of-experiments study to relate process parameters to residual-stress distributions and distortion, showing that different parameter combinations can produce fully dense parts and similar oriented microstructures, while distortion may depend more on stress gradients than average residual stress. These observations support screening with minimal single tracks, followed by a small number of compact bulk specimens or cubes for density and microstructure validation, while accounting for powder characteristics because powder size, shape, flow, and composition affect part quality.

First, use normalized process maps to identify a broad processability window rather than experimentally testing the entire parameter space. contexts.context: The excerpt supports a staged, powder-efficient experimental strategy for LPBF parameter optimization. Single scan tracks (SSTs) are presented as a simpler and faster preliminary screening method than producing bulk specimens. SST experiments use a single laser track on one powder layer, allowing laser power and scan speed to be varied systematically to identify a narrow processable P–v window while consuming very little powder. Track quality can be assessed by metallographic cross-sections, measuring geometrical features such as width, growth, and depth to evaluate melting and consolidation. To reduce preparation effort and material use further, an on-top analysis can assess the regularity of track borders without cutting and polishing the substrate; automation is desirable to reduce operator-dependent visual assessment. After narrowing the P–v range, subsequent experiments could use small density cubes or other compact bulk specimens to optimize hatch distance, layer thickness, scanning strategy, and volumetric energy density (VED). The excerpt cautions that VED is useful for organizing parameter studies but identical VED values can arise from different parameter combinations and produce different outcomes. Insufficient energy can cause balling, unmelted particles, and lack of fusion, while excessive energy can cause keyholing or evaporation. Thus, a sequential SST-to-small-cube design is more efficient than testing many full-size specimens, especially when powder is limited to roughly 100–300 g.

contexts.context: The excerpt supports a powder-efficient, staged experimental strategy for LPBF optimization. Because LPBF systems involve many parameters, experiments should initially focus on the most influential variables: laser power, scan speed, scan strategy, hatch distance, and layer thickness. Single-track experiments are particularly appropriate when powder is limited: the study used short, straight 3 mm tracks on a grit-blasted 316L substrate while varying laser power and scan speed, enabling rapid screening of melt-track continuity, width, depth, and morphology with minimal material. Volumetric energy density (VED), defined as P/(vσt), can provide a compact way to organize a parameter study, but it should not be treated as universally sufficient because different parameter combinations can produce the same VED yet different melting behavior. A practical design would therefore use a screening design over laser power and scan speed, include several parameter combinations at comparable VED values, and reject conditions showing lack-of-fusion or keyhole behavior. After identifying a stable single-track window, a small number of small cubes or pillars can validate density and porosity under selected conditions. For 316L, the excerpt reports stable-track/full-density-related VED values broadly around 100–1000 J/mm³, while values above 1000 J/mm³ may cause inefficient melting or keyholing. The excerpt does not specify a 100–300 g powder budget or a formal DOE methodology.

answer.formatted_answer:
Question: We will print nine different aluminium alloys, each as single tracks, density cubes and sub-size tensile bars, on an Aconity MIDI laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) machine (single-mode fibre laser, 400 W class with up to 1 kW optional, spot about 80 um, argon, build-plate heating available; a high-temperature heating module may reach 500 C or more). Powder is ultrasonically atomized in-house, sieved to about 20-63 um (D50 about 45-55 um), 100-300 g per alloy, so layers of 30-50 um and a reduced build platform. Please review the literature and give starting process windows and what build-plate heating does, per alloy family, quantitatively.

Alloy families: (1) AlSi10Mg; (2) Scalmalloy-type Al-Mg-Sc-Zr; (3) Al-Mn-Cr-Zr and Al-Mn-Ti-Zr; (4) Al-Mg-Zr (Addalloy-type); (5) Al-Fe-Zr (Aheadd CP1-type) and Al-Fe-Mg-Zr; (6) high-Mg Al-Mg-Si(-Mn) eutectic-type; (7) Al-Mg-Er-Zr; (8) Zr-modified 7xxx (Al-Zn-Mg-Cu-Zr) and 2xxx; (9) Al-Ce and Al-Ni eutectic alloys.

1. Published parameter sets on Aconity machines (MIDI, MIDI+, MINI, LAB, TWO) for aluminium alloys: laser power, scan speed, hatch, layer thickness, spot size, scan strategy, preheat, gas flow, resulting density. Include AlSi10Mg, Scalmalloy, 6061, 7075, 2024, Al-Mn-Sc, Al-Ce and any novel alloys. Which universities run Al on Aconity machines?
2. For each family above: the published crack-free, >99.5 % dense windows on any 200-400 W machine with a 70-100 um spot (power, speed, hatch, layer, volumetric energy density, plate temperature), and how the window shifts for 50 um layers and coarser powder.
3. Build-plate heating: for each family, the measured effect of 25 C vs 100-200 C vs 300-500 C plate temperature on (a) solidification and liquation cracking, (b) density and hydrogen porosity, (c) residual stress and distortion, (d) as-built strength (in-situ ageing or over-ageing: Si network coarsening in AlSi10Mg, Al3(Sc,Zr) precipitation in Scalmalloy at 200 C, Mn/Cr/Zr supersaturation loss), (e) Mg and Zn evaporation, (f) powder caking / sintering and reuse. Which families need a heated plate, which are indifferent, and which are harmed? Give the best plate temperature for each. Include the 6061 at 500 C result (Uddin et al.) and similar high-preheat studies for 7075 and 2024.
4. How to set a first print window for an alloy nobody has printed: normalized-enthalpy and keyhole-threshold criteria, lack-of-fusion criteria from melt-pool width/depth, Eagar-Tsai / Rosenthal estimates and their accuracy for Al (absorptivity values to use for Al alloys with powder, about 0.2-0.6 depending on mode), balling / humping limits at high speed, and how alloy thermal conductivity (e.g. Mn/Cr/Fe-rich alloys with low conductivity versus high-conductivity dilute alloys) and Mg/Zn vapour pressure move the window.
5. Efficient experimental designs when powder is scarce (100-300 g per alloy): single tracks on bare plate or on a thin powder layer, number of tracks per composition, small cubes (5-10 mm), mini tensile geometries (ASTM E8 sub-size, SS-J3, miniature dog-bones) and how their strength and elongation compare with full-size bars; reduced build-volume inserts; multi-material / multi-powder plates; in-situ alloying shortcuts. What is the minimum powder to get density + hardness + three tensile values?
6. Scan strategy and other settings that matter for novel Al alloys: 67 degree rotation, stripes vs chessboard, remelting, contour scans, oxygen level in the chamber (below 100-500 ppm), gas flow, recoater type for coarser / less flowable powder, powder drying (humidity; hydrogen porosity), and the effect of oxygen content of the powder.
7. Direct-ageing schedules after printing for each family and expected hardness / yield response; whether to stress relieve.
8. A recommended starting table for the nine families on an Aconity MIDI with a 20-63 um powder: layer thickness, power, speed, hatch, plate temperature, expected melt-pool depth/width, expected density, main failure mode to watch for, and a compact 12-20 condition design of experiments around that centre.

Give DOIs. Separate measured data from extrapolation.

## LPBF Processing of Nine Aluminium Alloy Families on the Aconity MIDI: Literature-Based Starting Windows, Build-Plate Heating Effects, and Experimental Design Guidance

---

### 1. Published Aconity Machine Parameters for Aluminium Alloys

The principal group operating aluminium alloys on Aconity platforms is the **University of Innsbruck, Department of Mechatronics, Chair of Materials Science** (Schimbäck, Kaserer, Mair, Riener, Leichtfried, Pogatscher and co-workers). Their Aconity MIDI is equipped with a 1000 W Yb:YAG laser and a resistive build-platform heater rated to 800 °C (schimback2024advancementsinmetal pages 2-3, schimback2022animprovedprocess pages 3-4).

**Scalmalloy® on Aconity MIDI** (measured): P = 370 W, v = 1000 mm/s, h = 100 µm, t = 30 µm, bilinear stripe pattern (5 mm stripe width), 67° rotation, argon atmosphere. Two build-plate conditions were investigated: no heating (NoBPH) and 200 °C (BPH). The 200 °C condition was specifically designed to promote in-situ Al–Sc–Zr solute-cluster formation during the build, yielding high as-built strength without subsequent heat treatment (schimback2024advancementsinmetal pages 2-3, schimback2022animprovedprocess pages 3-4). Process absorption for thermal simulation was set to 0.5 with a Goldak heat-source radius of 70 µm and depth of 100 µm (schimback2024advancementsinmetal pages 2-3).

**Al–Mn–Ti–Zr on Aconity MIDI** (measured, same group): P = 380 W, v = 1900 mm/s, h = 100 µm, t = 30 µm, 67° rotation stripe scan, no preheat. This produced crack-free specimens with as-built YS = 284 ± 3 MPa, UTS = 320 ± 1 MPa, and elongation 16.9 ± 0.2% (mair2022microstructuralfeaturesand pages 1-2).

**AlSi40 on Aconity Mini** (measured, Wilsnack et al.): 200 W max laser, 20–63 µm powder, substrate preheating at 400 °C (initially tested at 500 °C, which induced defect accumulation). Build chamber Ø98 × 130 mm³ (wilsnack2023fabricationofan pages 1-3).

**6182 on AconityONE** (measured, Riener et al.): Four 700 W Nd:YAG lasers, nitrogen atmosphere. A d-optimal DOE varying power, speed, hatch, focus position and preheat from 200–500 °C was performed. The 500 °C condition produced crack-free, fully equiaxed specimens with density >99.0% (riener2022processabilityofhighstrength pages 1-2, riener2022processabilityofhighstrength pages 10-12). DOI: 10.1007/s00170-022-08673-8.

**Other Aconity Al users**: Politecnico di Milano (Aconity MIDI+ for multi-material with pyrometer monitoring) (schimback2022animprovedprocess pages 3-4) and additional thesis work using Aconity MIDI for defect characterization of aluminium alloys.

---

### 2. Crack-Free, >99.5% Dense Process Windows per Alloy Family

The following table compiles starting process windows for 200–400 W machines with 70–100 µm spots, distinguishing measured data from extrapolations. With 20–63 µm (D50 ≈ 45–55 µm) powder and 30–50 µm layers on the Aconity MIDI, recommended starting conditions are:

| Alloy family | Layer (µm) | Power (W) | Speed (mm/s) | Hatch (µm) | VED (J/mm³) | Plate T (°C) | Expected density (%) | Main failure mode | Direct-aging schedule | Key references |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|---|---|
| **1. AlSi10Mg** | 30 | 350–370 | 1300–1650 | 120–130 | 54–79 | 25–100 | >99.5 | Low energy: lack of fusion/balling; high energy: keyhole and hydrogen pores. Heating near 200 °C relieves stress but coarsens the Si network and lowers strength. | Direct age 160–180 °C for 6–12 h; alternatively alloy-specific T6. | Measured AlSi10Mg process-mode window and preheat response; MIDI values are a starting extrapolation. (clement2024investigationintothe pages 43-51, macias2020influenceonmicrostructure pages 1-5, leis2021processwindowfor pages 1-2) |
| **2. Scalmalloy-type Al–Mg–Sc–Zr** | 30 | 370 | 1000 | 100 | 123 | 200 beneficial; 25 if maximum supersaturation is wanted | >99.5 expected | Mg evaporation, condensate/spatter-induced lack of fusion, and keyhole pores at excessive normalized heat input. | 325 °C/4 h; approximately 172 HV, 468 MPa YS and 517 MPa UTS reported. A 200 °C plate can provide partial in-situ clustering/ageing. | **Measured on Aconity MIDI**, 1000 W laser installation; bilinear 5 mm stripes. (schimback2024advancementsinmetal pages 2-3, schimback2022animprovedprocess pages 3-4, cerri2024mainheattreatments pages 14-16, mehta2021laserpowderbed pages 10-11) |

(martucci2022theinfluenceof pages 2-4, mair2022microstructuralfeaturesand pages 1-2, mehta2022effectofprecipitation pages 1-3, mehta2023advancingnovelalmncrzr pages 1-3) |
| **4. Al–Mg–Zr, Addalloy-type** | 30 | 330–370 | 900–1200 | 110–130 | 71–125 | 25–100 | >99 expected; verify experimentally | Mg evaporation, unstable melt pool and spatter-induced lack of fusion; cracking if primary Al₃Zr nucleation is insufficient. | Screen 350–400 °C for 4–8 h; schedule is an **extrapolation** from reduced-Sc Al–Mg–Zr–Sc alloys and requires hardness-time verification. | Centre condition is extrapolated from related Al–Mg–Sc/Zr and Er/Zr alloys; reduced-Sc material reached 160 HV after 350 °C/24 h. (belelli2022investigationandcharacterization pages 8-14, guo2022microstructureandmechanical pages 1-2) |
| **5. Al–Fe–Zr (Aheadd CP1-type) / Al–Fe–Mg–Zr** | 30–60 | 350–380 | 1200–1600 | 100–130 | 30–106 | 100 for CP1; 25–100 for Fe–Mg–Zr | >99.7; 99.8 measured for Fe–Mg–Zr | Gas/keyhole porosity and incomplete overlap; excessive Mg increases evaporation porosity. Intrinsic hot cracking is low near the Al–Fe eutectic. | 400 °C/4 h: CP1 ≈310 MPa YS; Al–Fe–Mg–Zr ≈376 MPa YS and 406 MPa UTS. | CP1 measured at 370 W, 1400 mm/s, 130 µm, 60 µm and 100 °C; Fe–Mg–Zr window measured over 200–380 W and 600–2600 mm/s. (pauzon2022anovellaser pages 1-4, li2025precipitationevolutionaging pages 1-3, li2025precipitationevolutionaging pages 3-4) |

High-Mg Al–Mg–Si(–Mn), eutectic-type** | 30 | 300–370 | 800–1300 | 100–130 | 59–154 | Begin at 100–200; test 300–500 only if cracks persist | >99 possible only with suitable eutectic chemistry or grain refinement; **unverified on MIDI** | Solidification/liquation cracking, Mg evaporation, hydrogen porosity and powder caking at high preheat. | Composition-specific: screen 160–200 °C for Mg₂Si ageing; avoid assigning a final schedule before DSC/hardness curves. | MIDI centre is an extrapolation. High-temperature preheat suppresses cracking in 6xxx only near 500 °C but may reduce density and as-built strength. (li2024additivemanufacturingof pages 31-34, bradfordvialva2021developmentofa pages 113-115, riener2022processabilityofhighstrength pages 10-12) |
| **7. (guo2022microstructureandmechanical pages 1-2, guo2022microstructureandmechanical pages 2-3) |
| **8. Zr-modified 7xxx and 2xxx** | 30 | 300–370 | 800–1300 | 100–130 | 59–154; initially constrain to ≈60–90 | 100–200 for refined variants; 400–500 only as a controlled high-preheat trial | >99.5 may be achievable with effective refiners; conventional chemistry can remain cracked regardless of apparent density | Solidification and liquation cracking, Zn/Mg/Cu segregation, Zn/Mg evaporation and keyhole porosity. In unmodified 7075, 100–200 °C did not suppress cracks and 400 °C produced columnar crack networks. | Composition-specific T6/T7 after density and cracking qualification; direct ageing alone is unlikely to restore optimum properties universally. | **Starting extrapolation**, not a published universal window. Unmodified 7075 lost ≈1 wt.% Zn and 0.3 wt.% Mg; high preheat alone was ineffective. (velikajne2026influenceofbase pages 6-8, velikajne2026influenceofbase pages 8-11, velikajne2026influenceofbase pages 1-2) |

Hot-cracking susceptibility is generally low, but off-eutectic primary intermetallics can embrittle the alloy. | Usually no conventional age-hardening response; use stress relief or chemistry-specific precipitation treatment only after hardness screening. | Al–Ce study used 200 W/30 µm and 365 W/45 µm regimes, 68 µm spot, 67° rotation, argon and O₂ <0.01 vol.%; speeds/hatches here are starting extrapolations. (hesselmann2022effectofprecipitationforming pages 3-5) |


*Table: Recommended first-pass LPBF settings for nine aluminium-alloy families using an approximately 80 µm spot and 20–63 µm powder. The table distinguishes directly measured conditions from machine-transfer extrapolations and identifies the principal qualification risks.*

**Effect of 50 µm layers and coarser powder:** Increasing layer thickness from 30 to 50 µm generally requires higher power or slower speed to maintain melt-pool depth ≥ 1.5× layer thickness. The Al–Cr–Mo–Sc–Zr study demonstrated successful processing at 100 µm layer thickness with build rates of ~47 cm³/h, though at higher laser power and with correspondingly adjusted hatch spacing (agricola2025parameterstudyof pages 1-2). For the Al–Fe–Zr CP1 alloy, 60 µm layers with 370 W and 1400 mm/s achieved >99.7% density (pauzon2022anovellaser pages 1-4). Coarser powder (D50 ~50 µm) tends to produce rougher layers and may require lower recoating speed; the process window generally narrows because the thicker effective layer reduces melt-pool overlap. The AlSi10Mg process window scales with the ratio P/d_b, where the optimum range was identified as P/d_b = 2000–5200 W/mm, centered around 3000–3500 W/mm for key-bowl melting with low porosity (leis2021processwindowfor pages 1-2).

**Key quantitative results:**

**(a) Solidification and liquation cracking:**
- AlSi10Mg: inherently crack-free regardless of preheat.
- 6182 at 500 °C: fully equiaxed grains (mean ECD 19.46 µm vs 33.72 µm at 200 °C), crack-free (riener2022processabilityofhighstrength pages 10-12). At 400 °C, initial equiaxed formation appeared (ECD 25.35 µm) but crack elimination was incomplete.
- 7075: preheating at 25, 100, 200, and 400 °C was systematically studied. At 200 °C, neither crack density nor grain morphology changed significantly. At 400 °C, crack networks transitioned to columnar morphology, but cracks were not eliminated (velikajne2026influenceofbase pages 6-8, velikajne2026influenceofbase pages 8-11, velikajne2026influenceofbase pages 1-2). DOI: 10.3390/ma19050970.
- 6061 at 500 °C (Uddin et al.): crack-free parts achieved, but as-built mechanical properties were low (YS ≈ 60 MPa, UTS ≈ 130 MPa, elongation 15%). After T6 treatment, strength recovered to YS ≈ 280–290 MPa and UTS ≈ 310–315 MPa, with reduced elongation (3.5–5.4%) (li2024additivemanufacturingof pages 31-34, bradfordvialva2021developmentofa pages 113-115).

**(b) Density and hydrogen porosity:**
- AlSi10Mg at 150 °C showed higher measured porosity (1.7% vs 0.9% at ambient) (zhu2023microstructuralanalysisof pages 3-5).
- 6182 at 500 °C: maximum density 99.0%, but density generally decreased with increasing preheat due to pore coalescence via Ostwald ripening (riener2022processabilityofhighstrength pages 10-12).
- For hydrogen porosity, all Al alloys benefit from powder drying (353 K/4 h documented for Al–Mn–Cr–Zr) (mehta2022al–mn–cr–zrbasedalloystailored pages 10-10).

**(c) Residual stress and distortion:**
- AlSi10Mg: at 200 °C, residual stress dropped from ~50 MPa (tensile) to negligible (macias2020influenceonmicrostructure pages 1-5).
- 7075 at 400 °C: pronounced stress relaxation, with GROD (grain reference orientation deviation) maps indicating substantially lower internal strain (velikajne2026influenceofbase pages 8-11).

**(d) As-built strength (in-situ ageing effects):**
- AlSi10Mg at 200 °C: Si-rich eutectic network coarsened and thickened, the heat-affected zone doubled in thickness, and strength decreased relative to no-preheat builds (macias2020influenceonmicrostructure pages 1-5, macias2020influenceonmicrostructure pages 5-9).
- Scalmalloy at 200 °C: in-situ cluster formation produced high as-built strength without post-treatment, eliminating the need for the standard 325 °C/4 h ageing step (schimback2024advancementsinmetal pages 1-2, schimback2024advancementsinmetal pages 2-3).
- Al–Mn–Cr–Zr: elevated platform temperatures risk consuming the Mn/Cr/Zr supersaturation intended for post-build direct ageing. Peak aging temperatures are 350–405 °C; uncontrolled exposure during long builds creates height-dependent properties (mehta2022effectofprecipitation pages 1-3, mehta2022effectofprecipitation pages 5-7).

**(e) Mg and Zn evaporation:**
- Scalmalloy: Mg burn-off is directly linked to normalized heat input; keyhole mode shows up to 1.2 wt% Mg loss vs 0.3 wt% in heat-conduction mode (schimback2022animprovedprocess pages 3-4). DOI: 10.2139/ssrn.4201040.
- 7075: approximately 1 wt% Zn and 0.3 wt% Mg were lost regardless of preheating temperature (25–400 °C) (velikajne2026influenceofbase pages 1-2).

**(f) Powder caking and sintering:**
- At ≥400 °C, Al powder sintering becomes significant, particularly for high-Mg alloys. AlSi40 at 500 °C on the Aconity Mini showed defect accumulation in lower layers, improved at 400 °C (wilsnack2023fabricationofan pages 1-3). Powder reuse after high-preheat builds requires careful re-sieving and characterization.

### 4. Setting a First Print Window for Novel Alloys

**Normalized enthalpy and keyhole threshold:** The normalized enthalpy is defined as β = AP / [ρ h_s √(π α v σ³)], where A is absorptivity, P is laser power, ρ is density, h_s is the heat content to reach melting, α is thermal diffusivity, v is scan speed, and σ is the Gaussian beam parameter (hong2026fittingfreediagnosisof pages 4-5). Melt-pool aspect ratio d/(w/2) classifies regimes: <1 conduction, 1–2 transition, >2 keyhole (hong2026fittingfreediagnosisof pages 4-5). For aluminium alloys, aim for the transition zone (key-bowl melting) for maximum efficiency and minimum porosity.

**Eagar–Tsai / Rosenthal models:** The Rosenthal point-source solution applies when beam radius r_b ≪ thermal diffusion distance; the Eagar–Tsai extension handles finite Gaussian beams by numerical integration of the temperature field, with melt-pool boundaries located at the liquidus isotherm via root-finding (hong2026fittingfreediagnosisof pages 4-5, francis2017theeffectsof pages 67-70). These models omit temperature-dependent properties and latent heat but are computationally fast and accurate to within a few percent in the conduction regime (hong2026fittingfreediagnosisof pages 4-5). For high-conductivity aluminium, the Rosenthal solution is especially applicable because conductive heat extraction is the dominant transport mechanism (bajaj2020precipitationduringintrinsic pages 60-63, bajaj2020precipitationduringintrinsic pages 58-60).

**Absorptivity values for Al alloys:** Bulk aluminium absorptivity at 1064 nm is ~0.06–0.12; powder absorptivity increases to ~0.2–0.4 due to multiple reflections. For thermal simulation of Scalmalloy on the Aconity MIDI, an absorption coefficient of 0.5 was used with a Goldak heat source (schimback2024advancementsinmetal pages 2-3). In the transition/keyhole regime, effective absorptivity can rise to 0.5–0.7 through multiple reflections within the vapour depression (hong2026fittingfreediagnosisof pages 4-5, martucci2023developmentandcharacterisation pages 21-23). A practical starting assumption: use A ≈ 0.3–0.4 for conduction-mode estimates and A ≈ 0.5 for Goldak-type simulations.

**Alloy thermal conductivity effects:** High-conductivity dilute alloys (e.g., Al–Fe–Zr with ~180 W/m·K after ageing) require higher linear energy for equivalent melt-pool depth. Mn/Cr/Fe-rich alloys with lower thermal conductivity (~120–160 W/m·K) have wider process windows because heat is retained in the melt pool longer (pauzon2022anovellaser pages 1-4, mehta2022effectofprecipitation pages 1-3).

**Mg/Zn vapour pressure effects:** High-vapour-pressure elements narrow the window toward lower energy inputs to minimize evaporation. The optimum for Scalmalloy lies in conduction-to-transition mode; keyhole mode causes up to 1.2 wt% Mg loss and melt-pool instability (schimback2022animprovedprocess pages 3-4). For 7075, Zn loss of ~1 wt% is essentially unavoidable at conventional LPBF parameters (velikajne2026influenceofbase pages 1-2).

**Balling/humping limits:** At high speeds with insufficient line energy, the melt track becomes discontinuous (balling). AlSi10Mg showed that P/d_b < 2000 W/mm leads to partial failure and balling (leis2021processwindowfor pages 1-2). This corresponds approximately to P < 160 W for an 80 µm spot.

### 5. Efficient Experimental Design with Scarce Powder (100–300 g)

**Three-stage protocol:**

**Stage 1 – Single scan tracks (SSTs):** Print single tracks on a bare substrate or thin powder layer, varying laser power (3–5 levels) and scan speed (5–8 levels) in a grid. Each track is ~10–20 mm long and consumes negligible powder. Assess track continuity, width, and depth from cross-sections. This identifies the stable P–v window and can be used to estimate hatch spacing from geometric overlap criteria (martucci2023developmentandcharacterisation pages 20-21, martucci2023developmentandcharacterisation pages 83-100, bertoli2018processstructurepropertiesrelationshipsin pages 35-39, bertoli2018processstructurepropertiesrelationshipsin pages 20-26).

**Stage 2 – Small density cubes:** Use 5–10 mm cubes (10 × 10 × 10 mm³ is a standard; each cube ~2.7 g for Al). A fractional factorial or Taguchi L9/L16 design with 3 factors (power, speed, hatch) at 2–3 levels requires 9–16 cubes (~24–43 g). Include 2–3 replicates at the centre point. Measure density by Archimedes or image analysis (chia2022processparameteroptimization pages 11-13, yadegari2025aluminumlaseradditive pages 19-21).

**Stage 3 – Sub-size tensile bars:** ASTM E8 sub-size specimens (gauge 25 × 6 × 6 mm or thinner, ~6–8 g each). Three tensile bars minimum per condition require ~18–24 g. SS-J2 miniature specimens (~0.5 mm thick, ~12 mm gauge) can be used if material is extremely limited; note that SS-J2/SS-T geometries may slightly overestimate ductility and yield strength relative to full-size bars (juhasz2020inandexsitu pages 104-109). Alternatively, miniature dog-bones with 11.5 × 3.5 × 1 mm gauge section were demonstrated for the Al–Fe–Mg–Zr alloy (li2025precipitationevolutionaging pages 3-4).

**Powder budget estimate per alloy:** ~15 g for SSTs + ~40 g for cubes (16 × ~2.5 g) + ~30 g for 3 tensile bars + ~40 g for powder losses (filling, sieving) ≈ **~125 g minimum** for density + hardness + 3 tensile values. With 200–300 g, a second condition (e.g., different VED or plate temperature) is feasible.

**Reduced build-volume inserts:** Use a small-diameter build insert (Ø50–80 mm available for the Aconity MIDI's Ø170 mm platform) to reduce powder bed volume and waste.

**DOE approaches:** Taguchi L9 (3 factors, 3 levels, 9 runs), Taguchi L16 (up to 5 factors, 2 levels, 16 runs), or Central Composite Design (3 factors, 15–20 runs including axials and centre points) are efficient (chia2022processparameteroptimization pages 11-13, yadegari2025aluminumlaseradditive pages 19-21). A compact 12–20 condition DOE around the starting-table centre point should vary power (±15–20%), speed (±20–30%), and hatch (±15%), holding layer thickness constant at 30 µm initially.

### 6. Scan Strategy and Other Critical Settings

**Scan rotation:** 67° layer-to-layer rotation is the near-universal standard for Al LPBF, documented for Scalmalloy, Al–Mn–Ti–Zr, Al–Mn–Cr–Zr, Al–Fe–Zr CP1, Al–Ce, and Al–Mg–Er–Zr alloys (hesselmann2022effectofprecipitationforming pages 3-5, mair2022microstructuralfeaturesand pages 1-2, pauzon2022anovellaser pages 1-4, guo2022microstructureandmechanical pages 1-2).

**Stripe vs chessboard:** Stripe (island) scanning with 5–10 mm strip width is standard; shorter scan vectors reduce residual stress. The Scalmalloy study on the Aconity MIDI used bilinear 5 mm stripes and found that restricting scan vector angle relative to the gas flow direction is important to reduce vapour-plume/laser interaction and spatter (schimback2024advancementsinmetal pages 2-3, schimback2022animprovedprocess pages 3-4).

**Oxygen level:** Maintain O₂ < 100–500 ppm (0.01–0.05 vol%). Al–Ce alloy processing used O₂ < 0.01 vol% (hesselmann2022effectofprecipitationforming pages 3-5). Lower oxygen is particularly critical for high-Mg alloys where oxide formation at the melt surface affects wetting and spatter.

**Gas flow:** Argon flow must be sufficient to clear the metal vapour plume and spatter from the processing zone. For Scalmalloy, Mg condensate deposits along the gas flow direction; scan vector orientation relative to gas flow affects Mg burn-off and spatter redeposition (schimback2022animprovedprocess pages 3-4).

**Recoater type:** Flexible rubber-lip or silicone recoaters are preferred for coarser or less flowable ultrasonically atomized powders. Rigid steel blades can displace or streak irregular particles.

**Powder drying:** Drying at 80 °C (353 K) for 4 h before printing is documented for Al–Mn–Cr–Zr powders and reduces hydrogen porosity from moisture-adsorbed hydroxyl groups (mehta2022al–mn–cr–zrbasedalloystailored pages 10-10). All Al powders should be dried, particularly high-Mg compositions where moisture promotes both hydrogen porosity and oxide growth.

**Powder oxygen content:** Higher oxygen content (from oxide shells on particles) affects melt-pool wetting and oxide inclusion formation. Ultrasonically atomized powder in an inert atmosphere should target O < 0.1 wt%; the Al–Fe–Zr CP1 powder contained 0.098 wt% O (pauzon2022anovellaser pages 1-4).

### 8. Recommended Starting Table and Compact DOE

The recommended starting parameters for the nine families on the Aconity MIDI with 20–63 µm powder are presented in the table above (artifact-00). To build a compact 12–20 condition DOE around each centre point:

**Suggested 16-condition fractional factorial per alloy (2^(4-1) = 8 main + 4 centre + 4 axial):**
- Factor A: Laser power (centre ± 15%, e.g., 315 / 370 / 425 W for Scalmalloy)
- Factor B: Scan speed (centre ± 25%, e.g., 750 / 1000 / 1250 mm/s)
- Factor C: Hatch spacing (centre ± 20%, e.g., 80 / 100 / 120 µm)
- Factor D: Plate temperature (2 levels: RT and recommended preheat)
- Layer thickness fixed at 30 µm
- Responses: relative density (image analysis on XZ cross-section), microhardness, crack density, melt-pool dimensions

**Build layout estimate:** 8 cubes (10 × 10 × 10 mm) + 4 centre-point replicates + 3 tensile bars per best condition ≈ ~105 g of Al per alloy, feasible within 200–300 g budget using a reduced-diameter build insert.

**Measurement priorities:** (1) Relative density by optical image analysis ≥ 6 images per orientation; (2) Vickers hardness HV0.3; (3) Crack density measurement for crack-prone families; (4) Tensile testing on best-density condition.

info.query:
We will print nine different aluminium alloys, each as single tracks, density cubes and sub-size tensile bars, on an Aconity MIDI laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) machine (single-mode fibre laser, 400 W class with up to 1 kW optional, spot about 80 um, argon, build-plate heating available; a high-temperature heating module may reach 500 C or more). Powder is ultrasonically atomized in-house, sieved to about 20-63 um (D50 about 45-55 um), 100-300 g per alloy, so layers of 30-50 um and a reduced build platform. Please review the literature and give starting process windows and what build-plate heating does, per alloy family, quantitatively.

Alloy families: (1) AlSi10Mg; (2) Scalmalloy-type Al-Mg-Sc-Zr; (3) Al-Mn-Cr-Zr and Al-Mn-Ti-Zr; (4) Al-Mg-Zr (Addalloy-type); (5) Al-Fe-Zr (Aheadd CP1-type) and Al-Fe-Mg-Zr; (6) high-Mg Al-Mg-Si(-Mn) eutectic-type; (7) Al-Mg-Er-Zr; (8) Zr-modified 7xxx (Al-Zn-Mg-Cu-Zr) and 2xxx; (9) Al-Ce and Al-Ni eutectic alloys.

1. Published parameter sets on Aconity machines (MIDI, MIDI+, MINI, LAB, TWO) for aluminium alloys: laser power, scan speed, hatch, layer thickness, spot size, scan strategy, preheat, gas flow, resulting density. Include AlSi10Mg, Scalmalloy, 6061, 7075, 2024, Al-Mn-Sc, Al-Ce and any novel alloys. Which universities run Al on Aconity machines?
2. For each family above: the published crack-free, >99.5 % dense windows on any 200-400 W machine with a 70-100 um spot (power, speed, hatch, layer, volumetric energy density, plate temperature), and how the window shifts for 50 um layers and coarser powder.
3. Build-plate heating: for each family, the measured effect of 25 C vs 100-200 C vs 300-500 C plate temperature on (a) solidification and liquation cracking, (b) density and hydrogen porosity, (c) residual stress and distortion, (d) as-built strength (in-situ ageing or over-ageing: Si network coarsening in AlSi10Mg, Al3(Sc,Zr) precipitation in Scalmalloy at 200 C, Mn/Cr/Zr supersaturation loss), (e) Mg and Zn evaporation, (f) powder caking / sintering and reuse. Which families need a heated plate, which are indifferent, and which are harmed? Give the best plate temperature for each. Include the 6061 at 500 C result (Uddin et al.) and similar high-preheat studies for 7075 and 2024.
4. How to set a first print window for an alloy nobody has printed: normalized-enthalpy and keyhole-threshold criteria, lack-of-fusion criteria from melt-pool width/depth, Eagar-Tsai / Rosenthal estimates and their accuracy for Al (absorptivity values to use for Al alloys with powder, about 0.2-0.6 depending on mode), balling / humping limits at high speed, and how alloy thermal conductivity (e.g. Mn/Cr/Fe-rich alloys with low conductivity versus high-conductivity dilute alloys) and Mg/Zn vapour pressure move the window.
5. Efficient experimental designs when powder is scarce (100-300 g per alloy): single tracks on bare plate or on a thin powder layer, number of tracks per composition, small cubes (5-10 mm), mini tensile geometries (ASTM E8 sub-size, SS-J3, miniature dog-bones) and how their strength and elongation compare with full-size bars; reduced build-volume inserts; multi-material / multi-powder plates; in-situ alloying shortcuts. What is the minimum powder to get density + hardness + three tensile values?
6. Scan strategy and other settings that matter for novel Al alloys: 67 degree rotation, stripes vs chessboard, remelting, contour scans, oxygen level in the chamber (below 100-500 ppm), gas flow, recoater type for coarser / less flowable powder, powder drying (humidity; hydrogen porosity), and the effect of oxygen content of the powder.
7. Direct-ageing schedules after printing for each family and expected hardness / yield response; whether to stress relieve.
8. A recommended starting table for the nine families on an Aconity MIDI with a 20-63 um powder: layer thickness, power, speed, hatch, plate temperature, expected melt-pool depth/width, expected density, main failure mode to watch for, and a compact 12-20 condition design of experiments around that centre.

Give DOIs. Separate measured data from extrapolation.
